studies.title: Sent Down With The Truth
studies.meaning: Two sentences establish where the Book comes from and what it asks. The first is impersonal: the sending down of the Scripture is from God, described by two names, Mighty and Wise. The second turns direct and addresses one man, saying it was sent down to him with the truth. Then the instruction, and it is not to believe or to argue but to serve, with the whole of one's religion given to God alone. Source, addressee, response, in that order.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from years when the community was small and the argument was about where the Book came from rather than what it contained. Opponents attributed it to poetry, to soothsaying, or to a human teacher. The commentators report no specific occasion for these two ayat and read them as the surah's frame, since the demand for undivided worship set out here returns at intervals through the whole chapter.

keyTerms.note: A verbal noun from a form that carries repetition, so it suggests delivery in stages rather than a single drop. The same opening clause heads three other surahs, all of them concerned with where revelation originates.

From a root meaning to be unmixed, used of milk strained clear or metal refined of its ore. It describes the state of the worshipper rather than the act, so the demand concerns what else is in the intention.
The word covers both a system of belief and the debt or obligation owed to a superior. Handing over the whole of it, rather than a portion, is what this phrase asks for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had no bound book. The Quraysh knew scripture as something other peoples carried, met on the trade roads north, and the word for a written thing kept that foreign prestige. Meanwhile worship in the town was portioned out: a household might keep its own deity, a tribe another, and the sanctuary held many at once. Devotion given wholly to one recipient was the unusual demand, not devotion itself.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause that opens this surah, naming the sending down of the Book as from God the Mighty, begins three other surahs word for word: 40, 45 and 46. Az-Zumar itself is named for a single word meaning groups or throngs, and that word occurs in only two ayat of the entire Quran, both of them near this surah's close.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is presented as having a direction before it has a content: it descends, and its origin is named before anything it says is quoted. That ordering matters, because the argument of the surah will rest on authority rather than on persuasion. The response asked for is not assent but exclusive service, which treats belief as something enacted. The two names given, power and wisdom, cover the two doubts a hearer might raise.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the same clause word for word, then turns immediately to signs in the created world.
States the same demand in the plural, that they serve God with devotion made purely His.
Repeats the instruction to call on God with devotion wholly His, against open resentment.

studies.applyIt: Pick one act of worship you already do today and notice, before you begin, who else you would be pleased to have see it. Do not try to suppress the thought. Just name it. The word this passage uses is about a mixture being separated, and separating starts with knowing what the other ingredient is.

studies.title: Only To Bring Us Nearer
studies.meaning: The ayah records what the Meccans actually said, and it is not a denial of God. They agreed God exists and is supreme, and claimed their intermediaries brought them closer to Him. The dispute set out here is therefore about access, not existence. The answer comes in two parts. What is due to God is settled first, as a question that answers itself, and their claim is then handed to judgement rather than argued down. The closing clause names lying and ingratitude together.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh maintained a sanctuary that drew pilgrims and trade from across the peninsula, and the deities housed there were understood by many as go-betweens rather than rivals to the supreme God. The commentators broadly agree that this ayah quotes that self-understanding rather than caricaturing it. No specific occasion is reported; it belongs to the surah's opening argument about undivided devotion.

keyTerms.note: The adjective form of the same root used a line earlier for the worshipper, applied now to the religion itself. It describes something with nothing else stirred into it, as water runs clear or gold is refined.

A noun of closeness in standing rather than in distance, the position a courtier holds with a king. It exposes what the speakers wanted: not knowledge of God but place with Him, arranged by someone else.
The plural of a word covering protector, ally and next of kin. In tribal usage it named whoever would answer for you, which is precisely the role being assigned here to the intermediaries.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on patronage. A stranger entering the town needed a local protector to trade or even to be safe, and a weaker clan attached itself to a stronger one for the same reason. Approaching a chief through a man who already had his ear was ordinary business, not corruption. The religious arrangement described here copied the social one exactly, which is part of why it seemed obvious to the people using it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the nearness these intermediaries were meant to secure occurs four times in the Quran. Two of them fall in the surah immediately before this one, where the same term describes the closeness God grants directly to prophets. So the Quran does not dispute that nearness is worth wanting. It disputes the route.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes a religious argument seriously enough to quote it. That is a method as much as a courtesy: the claim being refused is one about mediation, and refusing it establishes that God is reachable without a broker. The final clause is also careful. It does not say God refuses to guide liars, but that He does not guide the one who is both a liar and ungrateful, which makes the obstruction a settled disposition rather than a single act.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the same defence, that these are our intercessors with God, and answers it directly.
States the alternative in one line: God is near, answering the caller who calls.
Asks why the supposed intermediaries gave no help at the moment help was needed.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you have been waiting to be given permission for, or waiting for someone better placed to raise on your behalf. Ask directly instead, today, in your own words. This ayah is about a habit of going through people, and the habit is easier to see in ordinary business than in worship.

studies.title: The One, The Prevailing
studies.meaning: The refutation is built as a concession before it is a denial. Had God wanted offspring, He could have selected from what He creates whatever He wished. The point is that any such choice would still be a creature, picked out, which is not what having a son means. The idea collapses on its own terms rather than being simply rejected. The ayah then closes with two names, oneness and irresistible power, and the second is the reason for the first.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The claim being answered was current in the town, since some Arabs described the angels as God's daughters, and the surrounding argument of this surah concerns intermediaries. Communities to the north and in Abyssinia held a different version of divine sonship. The commentators read the ayah as addressing the whole category rather than any one group, which is why it is phrased as a hypothesis and not as an accusation.

keyTerms.note: Not merely one in number but one in a way that admits no second of the same kind. The article makes it a title rather than a count, so it excludes partners as well as offspring.
An intensive form from a root meaning to overpower completely. It appears five times in the Quran and each time stands beside oneness, so dominance is offered as the reason nothing shares in it.

A verb for picking the best from a larger set, used elsewhere of God selecting prophets. Its use here is deliberate: whatever was selected would already be part of creation, and so could not be a son.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Lineage was the spine of Arabian society. A man was placed by his father's name and his clan's, inheritance ran through sons, and a household without male heirs was genuinely exposed. Daughters were sometimes spoken of as a burden, which is part of what made the claim about angels insulting. To attribute offspring to God imported that whole structure of succession and need into a being described in the same breath as unshared.
studies.didYouKnow: The two names that end this ayah, the One and the Irresistible, occur together five times in the Quran and the second never appears without the first. Two of the five are in neighbouring surahs: this one, and again in the surah that follows, at the moment sovereignty is announced on the Day of Resurrection.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument proceeds by hypothesis rather than by assertion, which is unusual. Instead of saying God has no son, it grants the premise and shows the conclusion cannot be reached, since whatever God took would be something He made. That protects the claim from being merely a counter-assertion. The passage also ties oneness to power rather than to number, so the denial of partners becomes a statement about how nothing else can hold anything.

crossReferences.why: States the denial of offspring flatly, where this ayah arrives at it by argument.
Answers the same claim with the language of magnitude rather than of logic.
Ends with the same pair of names at the moment sovereignty is announced.

studies.applyIt: Notice one place where you talk about God using a shape borrowed from human life: a manager, a father, an accountant keeping score. The image is not wrong so much as small. Hold it against the second name in this ayah for a moment and see which parts of your picture do not survive the comparison.

studies.title: He Winds The Night Around
studies.meaning: Three acts are named in sequence and the middle one uses a verb found nowhere else in the Quran in this form. God wraps the night over the day and the day over the night, a coiling motion, one laid around the other the way cloth is wound. Then the sun and moon are put to service, each running to a term that is fixed and named. The ayah ends with power and forgiveness set side by side, which is not the pairing the description leads you to expect.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah arguing that the God the Quraysh already acknowledged as maker has a claim they were refusing. The commentators note that no one in Mecca disputed that God created the heavens and the earth; the surah's method throughout is to take the admitted premise and press on it. This ayah supplies the premise, and the ayat on either side draw the conclusion about worship.

keyTerms.note: From a root used for winding a turban or rolling something into a ball. The verb occurs in this form only here, and it makes the succession of night and day a wrapping rather than a swap.
A verb for setting something to work without wages, used of a labourer compelled to serve. Applied to the sun and moon it makes them workers on a schedule rather than powers to be courted.
Literally named rather than merely fixed, so the term has been specified by someone. The same word governs the world's end and a person's remaining days elsewhere in the Quran.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Time in Arabia was read off the sky. Caravans crossed at night by the stars and rested through the heat, the lunar month set the sacred periods when fighting stopped and the fairs opened, and a debt fell due at a named moon. The sun and moon were also worshipped by peoples the Meccans traded with. Calling them harnessed workers on fixed shifts was a demotion everyone listening would have felt.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb translated as wrapping here appears in this form nowhere else in the Quran. Its root returns only at the opening of surah 81, where the sun is said to be wound up at the end of the world. The same image of coiling therefore describes both the daily turning of the sky and its final undoing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Creation is presented as ongoing management rather than as a finished act. The verbs are present and repetitive: wrapping, wrapping again, running. That matters for the surah's argument, because a God who set the world going and withdrew could plausibly be approached through deputies, while a God still turning the sky each night could not. The closing names then attach forgiveness to exactly that continuing power.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same covering of day by night, there as pursuit rather than as winding.
Gives the sun and moon their courses in more detail, each swimming in an orbit.
Repeats the harnessing of sun and moon to a named term and draws the same conclusion.

studies.applyIt: Watch one of the two changeovers today, sunrise or sunset, for the whole two or three minutes it takes rather than glancing at it. Notice that there is no seam anywhere in it. The verb in this ayah is about winding one thing around another, and the absence of an edge is exactly what it describes.

studies.title: Formation After Formation
studies.meaning: The ayah moves from the first human being to the person being addressed without a break. One soul, then its mate from it, then livestock in eight kinds, then you in your mothers' wombs, creation after creation inside a threefold darkness. Commentators differ on what the three coverings are, most naming the womb, the enclosing membrane and the belly, and they treat the number as a measure of depth. The list ends by naming God as your Lord and asks one question: so where are you being turned.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is pressing the point that the God the Quraysh acknowledged as maker holds an exclusive claim on worship, and this ayah puts the argument in the most private place available, inside the body of the listener's own mother. No specific occasion is reported. The eight kinds of livestock refer to the four pairs of grazing animals set out at length in an earlier Meccan surah.

keyTerms.note: The phrase repeats one noun rather than listing stages, so it describes a sequence of complete makings rather than a single thing gradually filling out. Each stage is finished before the next begins.

A plural where English expects a singular, used through the Quran for layered obscurity, of night, of storms, of the deep sea. Here it is counted, and nowhere else in the Quran is darkness given a number.
A word covering either member of a pair, spouse or counterpart. It links the mate made from the first soul to the eight paired animals, so household and herd fall under one term.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Livestock were capital. A family's standing, its ability to marry sons off, its survival through a drought year all sat in the camels, sheep, goats and cattle it could count. Herds were reckoned in pairs because pairs were what produced more. Setting the making of a child beside the sending down of the herds put the two things a household most depended on into a single sentence, which is how the listener would have heard it.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only ayah in the Quran that puts a number on darkness. The plural form for layered dark occurs many times over, of night, of the sea, of a storm at sea, but nowhere else is it counted. The commentators' readings of the three layers differ in their detail while agreeing that the point is depth of concealment rather than anatomy.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage establishes that the most hidden process a person can name is not hidden. It works by scale rather than by assertion, since one sentence holds the first human being, the world's herds and a single embryo, with one Lord over all three. The closing question then turns rhetorical force into an accusation. It does not ask why you disbelieve but who is turning you, which implies a hand at work.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the stages of formation in detail and arrives at the same astonishment.
Lists the four pairs of livestock that the eight kinds here refer back to.
Opens with the same creation from one soul and its mate, drawing a social conclusion.

studies.applyIt: Ask one older relative what they remember of the pregnancy you arrived from: what the year was like, what was hard, what they feared. You were being formed through all of it and remember none of it. This ayah says the hidden part of your making was never hidden from God, and hearing the visible part from someone else makes that easier to sit with.

studies.title: No One Carries Another's Load
studies.meaning: Four claims arrive in sequence and are not obviously about the same thing. God has no need of you. He is not pleased by ingratitude in those who serve Him, and is pleased by thankfulness. No one bearing a load bears another's. Then return, disclosure, and knowledge of what chests hold. Commentators read the middle statement as the hinge: since God gains nothing either way, His displeasure at ingratitude is for the ingrate's own sake, and the burden clause explains why nobody else can absorb the cost.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators note that opponents of the message would tell those they were pressuring to follow them and let the consequence fall elsewhere, an offer answered in almost these words in another Meccan surah. Whether or not that lies behind this ayah in particular, the setting is a community under pressure from its own kin, where a promise that someone else would take the blame carried real force.

keyTerms.note: An adjective for one rich enough to require nothing from anyone. Used of God it denies not only need but the possibility of benefit, which changes what the clauses after it can be saying.

A feminine active participle, literally one who carries a load, with the word for the load itself standing beside it. The image is a porter or a pack animal, and the sentence denies transfer, not help.
Literally the possessor of the breasts, an idiom for the thoughts and intentions a person keeps inside. It closes a list about deeds by moving to what was never done or said aloud.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tribal life ran on shared liability. Compensation for a killing was raised across a whole clan, a debt could be answered by kinsmen, and a man's disgrace attached to relatives whether they consented or not. Collective payment was not a metaphor but an accounting practice with named procedures. A statement that no one carries another's load cut against the most reliable social insurance those listeners had.
studies.didYouKnow: This sentence appears five times in the Quran, in surahs 6, 17, 35, 39 and 53, in the same words each time. It is among the most exactly repeated formulas in the text. Commentators read it together with a passage in surah 29 saying that those who mislead others carry their own loads and further loads besides, and find no conflict: what is added is still their own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two ideas are held together that usually pull apart. God needs nothing from His creatures, and God is displeased or pleased by what they do. The ayah resolves this by putting the whole stake on the human side, so the displeasure is real but the benefit is not God's. The burden clause then makes the arrangement individual, and the closing phrase extends it inward, covering not only what a person did but what they meant by it.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the clause and adds that a heavily laden soul's call for help goes unanswered.
Records the offer to carry another's sins and the reply that the offer is empty.
States the same independence: if everyone on earth disbelieved, God would remain free of need.

studies.applyIt: Think of a decision you are deferring because someone else is nominally responsible for it: a family arrangement, a sign-off at work, a shared account nobody reconciles. Take the smallest piece that is genuinely yours and settle that piece today. This ayah is not about blame but about accounting, and accounting begins by finding which column an item belongs in.

studies.title: He Forgets What He Prayed For
studies.meaning: A sequence is described with a precision that reads like observation. Hardship touches a person; he calls his Lord, turning back to Him; then a favour is granted and he forgets the very thing he had been calling about. The forgetting is the crux. It is not that he stops praying but that the earlier prayer is erased. What follows is worse than a lapse, since he sets up rivals to God and draws others after him. The reply given is short and cold.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah addresses people who acknowledged God in emergencies, and the commentators note the pattern the Quran describes several times: Meccan traders who prayed to God alone in a storm at sea and returned to their intermediaries once ashore. No single occasion is reported for this ayah. It stands immediately before the portrait of the night worshipper, so the two figures are set against each other.

keyTerms.note: An active participle from a verb meaning to return again and again to a place. It describes posture rather than words, and this exact form occurs only here, though the verb recurs through the surah.
A verb for granting something outright as a gift, with no expectation of return and no wage implied. Its use sharpens the ingratitude, since what was given was neither a loan nor a payment.
The plural of a word for a peer or a competitor in the same field. The Quran uses it for misplaced objects of worship, framing them as asserted equals rather than as helpful go-betweens.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sea travel frightened the Arabs who did it. The route down the Red Sea from the coast was profitable and lethal, and a squall in the narrows could end a season's investment along with the crew. Overland, a lost water skin or a raiding party did the same work. Everyone listening had prayed at least once with nothing left to try. The ayah is describing what happened after they got home.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for granting a gift outright appears twice in this surah, here and again much later in the same chapter, both times inside a description of the same ingratitude. The second occurrence supplies the sentence the ungrateful person says out loud, that he obtained it through his own knowledge. The surah gives the thought here and the words for it later.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates unbelief in memory rather than in reasoning. The man in it never argues himself out of anything; he simply loses hold of an experience he had. That makes the Quran's insistence on remembrance a practical remedy rather than a devotional flourish. It also implies that sincerity under pressure proves less than the person praying assumes, since the same figure is described as wholly sincere and then wholly forgetful.

crossReferences.why: Tells the same story at sea, with the vow made in the storm and broken on land.
Compresses it to one sentence: sincere at sea, associating partners the moment they are safe.
Repeats the pattern later in this surah and supplies the sentence the ingrate actually says.

studies.applyIt: Write down one thing you asked for during a bad stretch that you have since been given. Just the fact, with a date on it. Keep it somewhere you will come across it again, a note app or the back of a bookmark. The failure this ayah describes is not disbelief but a lapse of memory, and a written line is the ordinary remedy for those.

studies.title: Are Those Who Know Equal
studies.meaning: The comparison is left unfinished on purpose. One side is drawn closely. A person is devout through the watches of the night, prostrating and standing, wary of what is coming and hoping for mercy. The other side is never described at all. Then the question changes shape. It does not ask whether the devout and the heedless are equal. It asks whether those who know and those who do not are equal. The two pairs are quietly matched to each other, and the reader is left to finish the sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayat immediately before this describe someone who calls on God in trouble and forgets the whole episode once relief arrives. This ayah sets the opposite case beside that one without naming the first party again, which is why the comparison reads as though half of it has been removed. The surah addresses people who conceded God's existence and let the concession change nothing.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning sustained obedience, and used specifically of long standing in prayer. It describes duration rather than intensity, which fits an ayah measuring a person by hours rather than moments.
The divisions of the night as that society counted them. Using the plural places the devotion across the night rather than at one point in it, without naming any particular watch.
Caution taken by someone who has understood a danger, not fright. It is the alertness of a traveller in bad country, and it sits here in the same clause as hope without either cancelling the other.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The night was long and unlit. It was divided into named watches that people used to organise sleep and guard duty. Standing through them cost sleep, in a society where hard work began at first light. Knowledge in that world lived in memory, not on shelves. A person was counted learned by what they could produce and use, not by what they had read or owned.
studies.didYouKnow: The question about those who know and those who do not is among the most quoted lines in Islamic scholarship. It stands at the opening of countless books. It does not sit in a passage about study. It arrives in the middle of a description of somebody praying through the night. The link between the two is made by placing them together, not by explaining.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Knowledge is measured by what it produces, not by what is held. The person described knows something in the sense that they act on it. They act at an hour when nobody is watching. So knowing here means an understanding that has reached the body. Wariness and hope appear in the same clause. Neither is offered as the grown-up form that replaces the other.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same connection from the other end, awe of God arising among those who have learned.
Describes the same night hours and the same two motives, and then adds what such people give away.
Shows the pattern in full, reflection at night on the heavens and the earth reaching a conclusion.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you are sure is true and have not acted on. Not a large thing. Do the smallest act it implies before you go to sleep tonight: send the message, make the payment, throw the item away. This ayah treats knowing and doing as the same measurement, and one small action is enough to take the reading.
studies.explainEasier: One person prays through the night, worried about the life to come and hoping for God's kindness. God says that person is not the same as someone who does not know. Only people who think will remember this.

studies.title: God's Earth Is Wide
studies.meaning: Three statements, and the middle one is the one that surprises. Those who do good in this world have good; God's earth is wide; the steadfast are paid in full without any reckoning. Early scholars have long read the middle clause as pointing toward leaving: if a place makes it impossible to live as you should, the world is not small. The last clause then changes the arithmetic. Almost everything else in this surah is counted precisely, and this alone is described as paid without a count being made.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. By this point some of the community had already crossed the sea to Abyssinia. Others were weighing it. The classical sources tie the clause about the wide earth to leaving in general, not to any single decision. The setting of the surah fits that reading. It speaks to believers under pressure in a city where they could not live openly as they wished.

keyTerms.note: From a root joining beauty to benefit, so the verb covers doing right and doing it finely. What is promised in return uses the same root, which makes the sentence an echo rather than an exchange.
Room enough, from a root about capacity and ease. The same root gives the word for what a person can bear, so the width described is measured against what someone is able to do.

The word for arithmetic and for accounting, and also the word used of the final reckoning. Removing it here means the wage is not arrived at by a sum, which is unusual in a text that counts carefully.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leaving your town in that world meant leaving your protection with it. A man away from his clan had nobody to answer for him and nobody to avenge him. He had no standing anywhere he arrived. Distance was exposure, not freedom. Telling people in that position that the earth was wide was not travel advice. It offered a different protection in place of the one they were giving up.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the phrase about provision given without reckoning in several places and of several groups. Early scholars single out one thing here. It is attached to patience in particular. Patience is the one quality with no visible product for a watcher to count. So a reward without a sum is matched to a virtue that leaves nothing to add up.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reward here escapes measurement. That is striking in a text that counts with care elsewhere: a grain yielding seven hundred, the weight of an atom brought into view. Dropping the count for steadfastness says something about the quality itself. Steadfastness is made up largely of what is not done. The middle clause then keeps the passage from sinking into resignation. It names a way out.

crossReferences.why: Poses the width of the earth as a question to people who stayed where they could not practise.
States the same thing in the first person and draws the same conclusion: My earth is wide, so serve Me.
Describes what the steadfast receive and the sentence they are said to say when trouble lands.

studies.applyIt: Find one situation you have been enduring mainly because you assumed there was no alternative. Spend twenty minutes actually checking: the cost of moving, the other job, what the conversation would involve. You may end up staying. The ayah places a statement about width between two statements about reward, and the width is the part most people never test.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people who believe to keep doing what is right. Those who do good get good back. God's earth is wide, so there is always somewhere else to go. People who stay patient will be paid in full.

studies.title: I Was Commanded To Serve
studies.meaning: Four short statements, each opening with the instruction to say. Together they answer a demand to state a position. He is commanded to serve God with the whole of his religion given to Him; commanded to be first among those who submit; afraid of a great day's punishment if he disobeys; and he worships God, his religion made purely His. The repetition is the argument. Nothing new arrives between the first sentence and the last, which is what a refusal to negotiate sounds like.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators place these ayat against the proposals the sources record from the Quraysh, in which the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was offered wealth, rank or a shared arrangement of worship in exchange for softening the message. Whether or not that occasion attaches to this passage specifically, the surah repeatedly answers people who wanted the demand for exclusive devotion loosened. The reply comes in the first person, and it repeats.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb, so the agent goes unstated and the speaker is placed under an order rather than announcing a preference. Repeating it makes the position transferred rather than chosen, which is what a messenger is.
The phrase can mean first in time or foremost in rank, and the commentators record both readings without settling it. Either way it removes the option of standing back and letting others go ahead.
The same noun used in the opening ayat of the surah, here with a personal ending attached. The move from the religion to my religion places a general principle onto one named speaker.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan public life ran on negotiated settlements. Disputes over the sanctuary, over trade shares, over blood claims were resolved by intermediaries who found a form of words both sides could accept. A man who would not take an arranged compromise was, socially, a problem. These four sentences are a refusal delivered in the accepted style: brief, declared aloud, and repeated so that it could not be reported as anything else.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase asking that religion be made purely God's occurs ten times in the Quran, and three of them fall in this surah, at its second ayah and twice inside this short run of four. The surah that follows immediately carries two more. No other pair of neighbouring surahs concentrates the phrase in this way.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophecy is presented here as a relayed order rather than as an insight. The speaker does not say he saw something or concluded something; he says he was told, and the passive leaves God as the only possible commander. That makes the message impossible to renegotiate with the messenger, since he has no discretion in it. The admission of fear in the third statement then places him under the very judgement he is announcing.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same formula, that he was commanded to be the first of those who submit.
Gives a longer version of the same declaration, ending with turning the face to religion.
States the same demand in the plural, as what people were ever commanded to do.

studies.applyIt: Say out loud, once, what you actually believe about God, in your own words, in a sentence you would be willing to repeat to someone who disagrees. Not a formula and not a quotation. These four ayat are a position stated plainly enough to be reported accurately, and most of us have never put ours into words at all.

studies.title: The Loss That Is Obvious
studies.meaning: The first clause sounds like permission and is not. Worship whatever you like besides Him, a release that functions as a verdict, since what follows names the outcome at once. The losers are then identified by what they lose, and the list is unexpected. Not wealth or standing but themselves and their families. The final phrase calls it the manifest loss, using a word from trade for capital that does not come back, and the item written off is the trader.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayat just before this put the messenger's position in the first person; this one turns outward to the audience, and the commentators read the apparent permission as a dismissal issued after an argument has been exhausted. Losing one's family carried particular weight in a town where kin were a person's only security, and where the message was already dividing households against themselves.

keyTerms.note: A trading word for capital that does not come back, the exact opposite of profit. Its use turns the Day of Resurrection into an accounting, and the item lost turns out to be the merchant.
The word covers household, kin and the people one belongs among. Losing them is counted as a loss separate from losing oneself, so relationships are treated here as part of what is at stake.
An active participle meaning both clear in itself and making other things clear. Attached to loss, it says the verdict will need no explaining to anyone once it arrives.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's wealth came from caravans, and a caravan was a shared investment. Families pooled capital and split returns, so a season's failure could ruin several households at once. Everyone in the town knew what it was to hear that a venture had come back short. The vocabulary of profit and loss was the most ordinary language available, which is why the Quran keeps using it for the hereafter rather than reaching for something grander.
studies.didYouKnow: The ironic permission that opens this ayah is a construction the Quran uses more than once, always with the consequence attached immediately so that it cannot be mistaken for leave. The clearest parallel is in surah 41, where hearers are told to do whatever they wish and told in the very next clause that God sees what they do.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage defines loss without reference to punishment. What is lost is the self and the people attached to it, which makes ruin a matter of what a person no longer has rather than of what is done to them. That reframes the hereafter as a disclosure of a present condition. The ironic permission also establishes that the freedom is real, since the choice is not removed, only its consequence is named in advance.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same ironic permission, do what you wish, with the consequence attached in the next clause.
Names the same loss of selves and families, there spoken by the wrongdoers themselves.
Describes those whose scales come out light as having lost their own souls.

studies.applyIt: Take one relationship you have quietly stopped tending: a sibling you do not call, a friend you let drift after an argument. Send one message today with nothing asked for in it. This ayah counts the people attached to a life as part of what can be lost, and drift is how most of that loss actually happens.

studies.title: Canopies Above And Below
studies.meaning: The image is precise and strange: shaded layers of fire above them, and shaded layers beneath. The word ordinarily means shade, the thing that gives relief from heat, so the picture is of shelter built from the wrong material. Then the ayah names what it is doing. This is how God puts fear into His servants, an unusual admission that a description is designed to work on the hearer. The closing address is direct and possessive: My servants, so be wary of Me.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah alternates warning and reassurance at close range, and this ayah sits directly before an announcement of good news for those who keep away from false objects of worship. The commentators note that the vocative used here, My servants, is addressed in this surah to both audiences: to those told to be mindful, and later to those who have wronged themselves and are told not to despair.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for shade or an awning, used elsewhere of clouds and of shelter given by God. Made of fire, it turns the one relief a desert traveller looks for into the thing pressing down.
A causative verb, so the fear is produced deliberately rather than arising by accident. The ayah states the intention behind its own imagery, which the Quran does only rarely.
From a root meaning to shield oneself, so the sense is guarding rather than dreading. The object is God, which makes the protection something sought from the very one it is sought against.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shade was survival. A traveller crossing the Hijaz timed the whole day around it, resting under an awning or a rock face through the hours when the ground burned, and tents existed as much for shade as for privacy. A stall, a well, an acacia: the geography of a journey was a sequence of shaded points. Turning shade itself into fire removed the one thing a desert listener would instinctively reach for.
studies.didYouKnow: The address at the end of this ayah, My servants, occurs five times in the Quran and three of them are in this surah. The other two frame it: it is used earlier for believers told to be mindful of their Lord, and later to open the offer of forgiveness to those who have gone too far. The same phrase carries a warning and an amnesty.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah is unusual in explaining its own method. It gives a terrifying image and then says plainly that frightening is the purpose, which treats fear as an instrument used on people God calls His own rather than as the reaction of an enemy. The possessive in the closing address does the theological work: the warning is an act inside a relationship, not a threat delivered from outside one.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same address, My servants, to open an offer of forgiveness rather than a warning.
Describes Hell as bedding beneath and coverings above, the same enclosing arrangement.
Places the punishment above them and under their feet in almost identical terms.

studies.applyIt: Notice today the moment you reach for relief without deciding to: the phone, the second coffee, the scroll before sleep. Mark it once, without stopping it. This ayah works by taking the shape of relief and filling it with the wrong thing, and the first step in recognising that is simply knowing where your own reaching goes.

studies.title: Good News For Those Who Turn
studies.meaning: Two acts define the group being praised, and both are movements rather than opinions: keeping clear of what is falsely worshipped, and turning back to God. The word for the false object covers anything that oversteps its bounds, so avoidance is described as a distance maintained rather than a position held. Good news is then announced for them, and the ayah closes by instructing that it be given, so the announcement is made twice inside one sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This ayah answers the warning immediately before it, and the close alternation between two audiences runs through the whole surah. Some early reports attach the description here and in the ayah following to particular Meccans who had turned from the town's idols before the message reached them. The reports differ from one another, and the commentators read the description as general rather than as a portrait of named individuals.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to exceed all bounds, covering idols, tyrants and anything granted an authority it does not have. It describes a role rather than naming a particular object, which is why it is left broad.
Built from the word for a side, so the sense is putting a thing off to one side and staying clear of it. It describes distance maintained over time rather than a single act of rejection.
A noun from the root for skin, since news shows first in the face. It names the announcement rather than what is announced, and here the content is left entirely unstated.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: News travelled by messenger, and the messenger who brought good news was paid for it. A man riding in with word that a caravan was safe, that a son had been born, that a feud was settled could expect a gift on the spot, and there was a recognised term for that payment. The word used here belongs to that world, where an announcement was an event with a bearer, a moment and a reward attached to it.
studies.didYouKnow: The definite form of the word for good news used here occurs five times in the Quran. Three of them belong to a single episode, the visitors who came to Abraham with word of a son, and another promises good news in this life and the next. This is the fifth, and here the content of the news is never specified at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two acts named are ordered deliberately: leaving before returning. That sequence treats the clearing of a space as prior to what fills it, which is a claim about how a person actually changes. The ayah also declines to say what the good news is, and commentators generally leave it open, taking the withholding as the point. The promise is larger than any item that could be listed underneath it.

crossReferences.why: Names the same overstepping authority as what is rejected before belief in God is affirmed.
States the mission of every messenger in these two terms: serve God, keep clear of it.
Announces good news to those who stand firm, with angels descending to deliver it.

studies.applyIt: Identify one thing that currently gets a say in your decisions out of all proportion to what it is: a metric, an opinion, a running comparison with someone. Give it one day off. Do not argue with it, simply do not consult it. The word this ayah uses is for something that has overstepped, and the practical answer it gives is distance.

studies.title: Those Who Follow The Best
studies.meaning: The description is of a listening habit rather than a doctrine. They hear what is said and follow the finest of it, which the commentators read in a range of ways: the best of what is revealed, or the better of two permitted courses, or simply the finer of two things heard. The verdict arrives immediately, that these are the ones God guided, so the listening is presented as evidence and not as cause. Then a hard question: can you pull out someone already sentenced.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a stretch where the surah keeps setting two figures side by side and asking whether they are equal. The question that ends this passage is addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and the commentators read it as consolation for a man worn down by refusal rather than as a rebuke. By this point the Meccan years had produced settled opponents as well as converts.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb to hear that adds effort and intention, so it means listening rather than merely hearing. The distinction is exact in the language and disappears in most English translations.
A superlative with a pronoun attached, so it is the best of the very thing heard. Commentators differ over whether it means the finest part of revelation or the better of two available courses.
Literally those who have the core, from a word for the inner part of a nut or a seed. It names people who reach what is inside a thing, not simply people who are clever.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry was Mecca's public argument. Verses were composed, recited at the seasonal fairs, memorised by rivals and answered in kind, and a man's standing could rise or fall on how a single line was received. Audiences were expert listeners who could judge a phrase on one hearing. Praising people for what they did with what they heard was praising a skill the town already prized, and turning it toward a different content.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for people of understanding, literally those who possess the kernel, occurs in this exact form seven times in the Quran, and two of them are in this surah: here, and nine ayat earlier at the close of the question about whether those who know and those who do not are equal. Both times it ends the sentence rather than opening it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is described in reverse here. The passage does not say God guided them and so they listened well; it names the listening and then identifies them as the guided. That ordering keeps human effort visible without making it the cause, which is how the Quran generally handles the question. The second ayah then draws a limit around the messenger, whose responsibility ends at delivery and whose success is not his to secure.

crossReferences.why: Closes with the same phrase for people of understanding, after a comparison left unfinished.
States the same limit plainly: you do not guide those you love, God guides whom He wills.
Instructs attentive listening when the Quran is recited, using the same intensified verb.

studies.applyIt: The next time someone disagrees with you, wait until they have finished and then say back the strongest version of their point before you answer. Not the version that is easiest to dismiss. This passage praises people for what they do with what they hear, and hearing the best of it is a habit you can practise on an ordinary conversation.

studies.title: Chambers Above Chambers
studies.meaning: The ayah answers the sentence of ruin just passed with an image of height. Instead of listing pleasures it describes architecture: upper rooms, and above them more upper rooms, purpose-built rather than found, with water running underneath. Then the sentence stops describing and gives a guarantee. This is God's appointment, and He does not fail an appointment. Classical commentators read the doubled word as storeys stacked vertically, and note that the sentence ends on the reliability of the promise rather than on the scenery.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah that keeps setting two kinds of people side by side. The ayah before it has described those over whom the sentence of punishment is fixed, and this one opens with a word of contrast. The commentators report no specific occasion. The setting is the later Meccan years, when the small community had little property and no secure housing, and when building upward was something only the wealthy of the town could afford.

keyTerms.note: An upper room reached by stairs, the storey above the ground floor. Repeating the word puts one such room above another, so the picture is of height built on height rather than of width.
A passive participle from the verb for building. It rules out caves and natural shelter: these are made structures, raised deliberately, which is what the word adds to the picture.
Not merely a pledge but an appointment, a meeting fixed for a time and a place. The denial at the end is therefore about keeping an appointment, not only about telling the truth.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was a town of stone and mud-brick houses packed into a dry valley with no river and no field. Water came from wells and had to be carried by hand, sometimes up stairs. An upper room was a mark of means: cooler, out of the dust of the lane, and expensive to build. To promise storey upon storey with water running underneath was to promise the two things the valley itself could not supply.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for these upper chambers occurs only a handful of times in the Quran, at 25:75, 29:58 and 34:37 among them, and this is the single place where it is repeated inside one clause, chambers above chambers. The closing assurance that God does not fail His appointment closes its sentence the same way at 3:9 and 13:31.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The promise is not left to stand on how attractive it sounds. It is signed with a statement about God's character, which moves the ground of confidence from the desirability of the reward to the reliability of the one making it. The final clause also treats the future as an appointment rather than a possibility, so what has been described is scheduled rather than hoped for, and the reader's part is waiting rather than wishing.

crossReferences.why: Promises the same high dwellings with water flowing beneath them, there to those who work righteousness.
Names the same chambers and says what does not buy entry to them: neither wealth nor children.
The mirror image four ayat earlier, where what is stacked above and below is fire.

studies.applyIt: Next time you find yourself looking at a home you cannot afford, notice what the wanting actually feels like before you talk yourself out of it. Then read this ayah with that feeling still present. You are not being told that houses do not matter. You are being shown where the good version of that appetite points, and asked to keep the appetite while changing the address.

studies.title: From Springs To Debris
studies.meaning: One substance is traced through five stages: water falls, sinks, is threaded through the ground as springs, comes back up as crops of different colours, dries to yellow, and ends as broken stubble. Nothing is skipped and nothing is dramatised. The conclusion is placed at the end and addressed to people with understanding, which means the sequence itself is the reminder. Commentators note that the same run of verbs describes a human life, and read the ayah as a compressed argument rather than a scene.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is arguing with people who acknowledged God as creator but organised their lives around other powers, and it reaches repeatedly for agriculture, which its audience could check for themselves. No occasion is reported. The ayat around this one move between signs in nature and the hardening or softening of hearts, so the withering field is deliberately set beside the person who will not take a reminder.

keyTerms.note: A plural from a root meaning to gush. It appears nowhere else in the Quran, and it names the hidden stage of the cycle, water underground between the falling and the rising.
From a root for smashing. It is what is left when dry stalks are crushed by wind or underfoot, too broken to be gathered, and the word itself has the sound of the breaking in it.
The plural of the word for the kernel inside a shell, the part worth having. Used of understanding, it means the mind that gets past appearances to the thing itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had almost no rivers. Cultivation depended on rain that vanished into the ground and reappeared in springs, in the wells of oasis towns, and in the sudden green of a valley floor after a storm. A farmer watched a field turn from green to yellow to nothing within weeks. Anyone who had travelled a trade route had ridden past the same ground in both states and knew exactly how short the interval was.
studies.didYouKnow: The word translated springs occurs once in the entire Quran, here. The word for the crushed debris at the end occurs three times, here and at 56:65 and 57:20, and in both of those places it also describes a crop reduced to nothing. The ayah thus opens with a term used nowhere else and closes with one reserved for failed harvests.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument is not that the cycle is beautiful but that it is complete, observable, and ends in loss every time without the loss counting as a failure. That allows two things to be held together: the world is a genuine work of God, and it is not the thing to build a life on. Addressing the conclusion to those with understanding makes it a matter of attention rather than of information, since everyone has already seen this happen.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same field from green to yellow to debris, there as a description of the present life.
Gives the same parable of water, growth and scattering, applied directly to worldly life.
The next ayah turns from the withering field to hearts hardened against the reminder just given.

studies.applyIt: Find something in your home that is at the yellowing stage: a plant past its best, fruit going soft, shoes almost finished. Spend a minute with it without either throwing it out or rescuing it. You are looking at the third act of the sequence in this ayah, and the small work here is to see it as a stage rather than as a nuisance.

studies.title: A Chest Opened To Light
studies.meaning: The comparison is left unfinished. The ayah asks about the one whose chest God has expanded, walking by a light from his Lord, and never states what he is unlike. What follows instead is a warning to those whose hearts have gone hard at the mention of God. Commentators read the expansion as capacity, room made inside a person, and note that the light is described as coming from his Lord rather than generated by him. Hardness is its exact opposite: a surface nothing enters.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a city where the message had been heard for years and had produced both responses. Some had opened to it, some had set hard against it, and the surah keeps placing the two beside each other. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Its language of an expanded chest is the same used elsewhere of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) himself and of Moses asking for help before a task he dreaded.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to open something out and lay it flat, and it is also the ordinary word for explaining a difficult text. Applied to the chest it means room made inside a person, not an argument won.
From a root used of stone that has set and of ground baked past working. It describes a surface that no longer takes an impression, so nothing said can leave a mark on it.
Indefinite, so a light rather than the light. What the person walks by is described as issuing from his Lord, which puts the source outside him and makes the seeing a gift rather than an achievement.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan crossing at night navigated by starlight and by whatever moon there was; a man without light simply stopped where he stood until morning. In the same world stone was the material of permanence, used for the walls that outlasted the men who raised them. The two images in this ayah are the two conditions of travel: a person moving because he can see, and a person who has become part of the landscape.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb behind opened his chest occurs five times in the Quran. In four of them God is the one who opens, at 6:125, 20:25, 94:1 and here. The fifth, at 16:106, is the only place where a human being does the opening, and what he opens his chest to is rejection of faith.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The difference between two people is located below the level of argument. One has been given interior room and a light to walk by; the other has a heart set hard specifically against the mention of God. The ayah does not say the hardened were made that way, and the surrounding ayat hold them answerable. What it does say is that receiving guidance feels from the inside like space, and that refusing it feels like nothing at all.

crossReferences.why: States the same expansion as the mark of guidance, with a chest made narrow and constricted as its opposite.
Puts the same verb in the divine first person, as a favour already granted rather than a condition.
Describes hearts harder than rock, noting that rocks at least still split and let water through.

studies.applyIt: Pick one line of the Quran you have heard so often that it no longer moves anything, and read it slowly enough to get bored. The boredom is information. Then ask, without answering quickly, whether the line has stopped saying anything or whether you have stopped having room for it. You are not diagnosing yourself, only noticing which of the two it feels like.

studies.title: Skins Shiver Then Soften
studies.meaning: Three claims are made about the Book and then one thing is reported about its effect. It is the best of narrations; it is consistent, its parts resembling one another; and it is paired, doubling its themes and returning to them. Then a body appears in the sentence: skins that shiver at it, and the same skins and hearts softening afterwards toward the remembrance of God. Commentators differ over whether the paired quality means repeated stories or matched promise and warning, and record both readings.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been arguing about the source of the recitation, and here it makes a claim about its texture that the audience could test, since they were connoisseurs of speech who judged poets by ear at the seasonal fairs. What follows the description is not an argument but a report of what happens in listeners' bodies, which places the evidence in the hearing rather than in the debate. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: From the root for likeness. Here it does not mean ambiguous but uniform: the parts resemble one another in quality and none falls off, so no section betrays a different hand.
From the root for doubling or folding over. Commentators take it of themes that arrive in pairs and of matter that returns, and the word occurs in only one other place in the Quran.
A rare intensive verb for skin contracting into gooseflesh. It occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and it names an involuntary reaction, something the body does before the person has decided anything.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Speech was the art form of the peninsula, and a tribe's standing could rest on its poets. Verses travelled between markets by memory, were judged in public, and were quoted for generations afterwards. An audience trained that closely could hear a seam in a composition the way a jeweller sees a join in metal. A claim that this recitation held its quality all the way through was made to people equipped to test it.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for the shiver in this ayah appears once in the whole Quran. The word for the Book's paired quality appears twice, here and at 15:87, where it describes the seven oft-repeated verses. The ayah puts the two together to describe a reaction in two stages, contraction and then softening, so the fear is not treated as the destination.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is described as having an effect on the body before it has one on the will, which gives it a kind of evidence that argument cannot supply. The order matters as much as the content. The shiver comes first and does not stay; what it resolves into is softness toward the remembrance of God. That sets the emotional shape of the whole relationship, in which awe is real but works as a doorway rather than as the room.

crossReferences.why: The only other place the revelation is called paired, there of the seven oft-repeated verses.
Reports the same physical response, hearts trembling when God is mentioned and faith increasing at recitation.
Makes a matching claim about the Book's range, every kind of comparison set out for people.

studies.applyIt: Listen to a recitation of any length without a translation running alongside it, and pay attention to your shoulders and the back of your neck rather than to the meaning. Whatever happens or does not happen is fine. You are checking one claim in this ayah against one body. Do it once this week, at an hour when you are not already tired.

studies.title: Shielding With The Face
studies.meaning: The question is left unfinished again, matching the one two ayat earlier: is the man who has nothing left to guard himself with but his own face like the man walking by a light? Commentators explain the picture as a person whose hands are bound, so the most exposed and most protected part of the body becomes his only shield. The scene then closes with a sentence addressed to the wrongdoers, and the word for what they receive is the word for wages earned by work.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This is the closing half of a pair that began with the chest opened to light, and setting two figures side by side is how the surah argues throughout. No occasion is reported for either ayah. The audience was being warned about a day most of them denied outright, and the imagery here is drawn from ordinary humiliation, a man overpowered in a lane, rather than from anything cosmic in scale.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for putting something between yourself and harm; the noun for God-consciousness comes from the same root. Here the root that usually names protection describes a man with nothing left to protect himself with.
The face carried a person's honour, and covering it was the standard gesture of shame. Using it as a shield inverts that completely: the part most guarded becomes the part put forward first.
A commercial verb for acquiring by work or trade. Applied to deeds it makes the outcome wages rather than penalty, which is why the sentence says taste what you earned and not what you deserve.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a society run on honour the face was the visible seat of it. Men covered the lower face against sun and dust, and having one's face struck, or being made to press it into the ground, was the standard image of total defeat. Prisoners were bound at the wrists and led. A man with tied hands leaning his face into a blow was something everyone in that audience had seen or heard described.
studies.didYouKnow: Both halves of this comparison are left grammatically unfinished. The ayah two places earlier asks about the man whose chest was opened and never says what he is unlike; this one asks about the man shielding with his face and stops in the same way. The commentators supply the missing half in their explanations rather than treating the gap as an error.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two outcomes are deliberately not described in the same register. One is light and interior room; the other is a body with nothing left to put between itself and harm. Naming the second as wages keeps it continuous with the life that produced it rather than making it an external penalty imposed from outside. Taken with the ayah before it, the difference between people is presented as something already under way in them now.

crossReferences.why: The first half of this comparison, the chest opened to a light, which this ayah answers.
Shows the same posture, people gathered and driven upon their faces, as the picture of defeat.
Sets the same two figures against each other, one walking bent over and one walking upright.

studies.applyIt: Think of a moment when you were caught out and had nothing to say, and notice what your hands did and where your eyes went. That reflex is what this ayah is drawing on. There is no need to dwell on the memory. Just let it be the picture attached to these words the next time you hear this passage recited.

studies.title: From Where They Did Not Perceive
studies.meaning: Three sentences, each moving the argument on. Earlier peoples denied, and were reached by a punishment that arrived from a direction they were not watching, which is the detail the passage lingers over. Then the disgrace they tasted is placed in this life and immediately relativised: what comes later is greater. The third sentence changes register entirely and says why any of this is being told, that every kind of comparison has been set out in this Quran so people might remember. Warning is presented here as teaching.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience knew the ruined sites of earlier peoples along the trade roads running north and south, and the surah appeals to that knowledge more than once. No specific occasion is reported. The phrase about a blow from an unwatched direction fits a city whose security came from its position and its reputation, and which expected any real threat to be visible on the horizon days in advance.

keyTerms.note: A verb for sensing rather than knowing, the awareness that comes through the skin and the ear. The phrase says the blow arrived outside the range of their senses, not merely outside their calculations.
Not private guilt but exposure, the loss of standing in front of others. The word names a social punishment, which is why it is placed in the present life while the greater one is left for later.
Covers a likeness, a proverb and an illustrative case at once. Saying every kind of it has been struck means the Book has varied its method, not that it has repeated its point.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan caravans passed the remains of abandoned settlements, and stories of vanished peoples were part of the shared stock of northern Arabia. Security in that world came from knowing which direction trouble arrived from: raids came along known routes, at known seasons, by parties whose size could be guessed from their dust. A blow from an unwatched quarter was a specific professional fear, not a vague one.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about punishment arriving from where they did not perceive occurs three times in the Quran, here and twice in surah 16, where it describes a roof caving in on the people who built the house and a warning to those who scheme. In all three places the point is the direction of the blow rather than its severity.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Describing the blow as arriving from an unwatched direction says something about what security actually is: not a level of protection achieved, but a relation. The passage then refuses to make the historical examples its main point. They are material for a book whose stated purpose is remembering, which subordinates the threat to the teaching and gives the reader something to do with the story other than be frightened by it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase about a blow from an unwatched direction, there of a roof collapsing on its builders.
Describes the same surprise, ruin arriving from where it was not expected, at a fortified settlement.
Repeats the claim that every kind of comparison has been set out for people in this Quran.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you are quietly braced against and ask yourself where you are watching from. Most people guard one door carefully and leave the others. You are not being asked to guard them all, which is impossible. You are being asked to notice that your sense of safety has a shape, and that the shape came from you rather than from the facts.

studies.title: One Master Or Many
studies.meaning: The description of the recitation as Arabic and free of any twist leads straight into a small legal picture. Two servants are set side by side: one owned in shares by partners who quarrel with each other, one belonging to a single man. The question is whether they are alike, and no answer is given, only praise. Commentators read the first as the person answering to several claims at once, and note that the misery in the picture comes from the partners' disagreement rather than from the number of owners.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Servitude and joint ownership were ordinary features of the audience's world, and the comparison is drawn from a situation they could settle without instruction. The surah has been arguing against dividing devotion among several powers since its opening ayat, and this parable is its plainest statement of the case. No specific occasion is reported for either ayah in the classical sources.

keyTerms.note: Used of a bent stick and of a path that deviates. Denying it of the recitation claims straightness as a property of the text itself, not only truth in what it reports.
A rare word for partners who are difficult with one another and pull in different directions. It occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and it puts the trouble in the owners rather than in the man owned.
A noun used adjectivally for something free of any competing claim, from the root of soundness and peace. The same root gives the words for submission and for safety.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A servant held in shares was a real and awkward arrangement. Each owner had a claim on his time, and the man could be pulled between households, sent on errands that cancelled one another out, and blamed by everybody when nothing was finished. Arrangements of this kind arose often enough that the customary law of the time had procedures for them. The listener did not need the parable explained, only to picture the man's week.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the quarrelling partners occurs once in the whole Quran, here. The description of the revelation as an Arabic recitation, in these exact two words, occurs four times: here, at 20:113, 41:3 and 42:7. Each of those places attaches it to a purpose, that people may become mindful, or know, or be warned.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The case for one God is made here as a practical argument about coherence rather than a metaphysical one about number. A life answerable to several authorities who disagree is not richer than a life answerable to one; it is incoherent, and the incoherence is paid for by the servant. Read this way, devotion to one God is being described as the shape of a workable life, and its alternative as a description of being pulled apart.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase about an Arabic recitation, joined there to the purpose of understanding.
Also denies any crookedness in the Book, in the opening line of another surah.
States the position this parable answers, devotion divided among intermediaries said to bring people nearer.

studies.applyIt: Write down, in one line each, the three people or things you are most trying not to disappoint. Look at whether any two of them pull in opposite directions, and where you have been paying for the difference. This is not an instruction to drop anything. It is a way of seeing the shape this parable describes, using your own week as the picture.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: You Will Die And They Will Die
studies.meaning: The first sentence states the plainest fact available in the shortest possible form, addressed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and to his opponents together, with no consolation attached. The second says the argument now running does not end at the graves; it resumes before God, and the verb used is the one for parties bringing a case. Only then comes the judgement, put as a question about who could possibly be more wrong. Commentators note the order, since the verdict is reached by argument rather than asserted.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah belongs to the years when opponents in Mecca were waiting the movement out, expecting it to end with the man who carried it, and the commentators report that some of them said so openly. The passage grants the premise without arguing and then removes what they wanted from it, by saying that the dispute will simply be resumed in another place. No further occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: An active participle, so it names a standing condition rather than a coming event. The sentence does not say you will be killed or die soon; it says mortality is already true of him.
A verb for two parties bringing a case, from the root for an opponent at law. It keeps the quarrel running in Mecca intact and changes the venue rather than closing the file.
Truthfulness of speech rather than correctness of fact; the root is used of a person who keeps his word. Denying it is therefore rejecting a man's honesty, not merely disagreeing with a claim.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan disputes were settled before the tribe or by an agreed arbitrator, and a case could run for years while both sides waited for circumstances to shift. Death often ended one. An old feud might lapse simply because the man who carried it was gone, and his sons could take it up or let it drop as they chose. Waiting an opponent out was a normal and entirely respectable strategy.
studies.didYouKnow: The first of these three ayat is four words long in Arabic and is the shortest ayah in the surah. It contains no verb in the usual sense, attaching a participle for mortality to each of the two parties instead. The longest ayat of this surah run to more than thirty words, so the contrast in the running text is audible.
studies.theologicalSignificance: By making the messenger's mortality the premise rather than an objection, the passage separates the message from his survival. It also gives judgement a legal shape: not a sentence handed down on people who have said nothing, but a case in which both parties appear and speak. The gravest wrong then named is a wrong of speech, inventing about God and rejecting a truthful man, which locates the fault in what people say rather than in what befalls them.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same point about the messenger's death, there as a warning against turning back afterwards.
Answers those waiting for him to die by noting that no human before him was granted permanence.
Shows the dispute continuing among the parties themselves after arrival, followers turning on those they followed.

studies.applyIt: Think of an argument you are currently waiting out rather than settling, hoping distance or time will close it for you. Do not resolve it today. Just be honest with yourself about which of the two you are doing, and then write the other person's strongest point in one sentence, in their words rather than in yours.

studies.title: Bringing And Confirming The Truth
studies.meaning: Two verbs stand side by side and both are needed: bringing the truth, and confirming it. Commentators read the first of the one who carries a message and the second of the one who accepts it, and many take the pair together as a description of anyone who says what is true and then stands behind it. What follows is unusually open. They have whatever they wish with their Lord, unitemised, which is rare, and it is named as the return for doing good rather than for being right.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah just before this pair has named the worst of wrongs as lying about God and rejecting a truthful man, and this is its exact mirror, which is how the surah usually proceeds. The classical commentators record several readings of who is meant, ranging from the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and those who believed him to every truthful speaker and every honest hearer, and they leave the range open.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of the root behind truthfulness, meaning to declare a thing true and to act as though it is. The same root gives the word for charity, where belief is proved by outlay.
From the verb for shielding oneself. It names people who keep something between themselves and harm, so the English word righteous misses the caution the Arabic actually carries.
From a root meaning both beautiful and good, so it describes doing a thing well rather than merely doing the right thing. The reward is attached to that word, not to correctness of belief alone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In an oral culture a claim travelled on the credit of the man carrying it. Merchants, messengers and poets were assessed for reliability the way goods were assessed for weight, and a man known to shade his reports lost work and standing together. Pairing the bringing of a truth with standing behind it described a practical reputation, the kind a listener had been judging in other people all his working life.
studies.didYouKnow: Both verbs in the first of these two ayat come from a single Arabic root. So do the words for truthfulness, for a bridal gift, and for charity. The root's underlying sense is of something solid all the way through, which is why one family of words can describe speech, a person and a payment without strain.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Righteousness is defined here by a relation to truth rather than by a list of acts, and it takes two forms that need each other, since someone must carry a truth and someone must receive it. The reward is left unspecified, which makes it a statement about God's generosity rather than a description of a place. The final clause then shifts the term from truthful to good-doing, quietly refusing to let truth stay a matter of assent.

crossReferences.why: The mirror of this pair: inventing about God, and rejecting the truth at the moment it arrives.
Uses the same open-ended promise, whatever they wish, and then adds that there is more besides.
Ranks those of proven truthfulness immediately after the prophets among the people God has favoured.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you say you believe and find the smallest place this week where saying it will cost you something minor: a correction you would rather not make, a claim you would rather not walk back. Do that one. The ayah pairs carrying a truth with standing behind it, and standing behind it is usually small, awkward, and unwitnessed.

studies.title: The Worst Removed, The Best Rewarded
studies.meaning: An exchange is described whose two halves deliberately do not match.
