What is taken away is the worst of what a person did; what the reward is measured by is the best of what they did. Commentators note that the first verb means covering over rather than declaring innocent, and that the two superlatives carry the argument: if the worst is removed, everything beneath it goes with it, and if the best sets the rate, everything is paid at that rate. The sentence is a purpose clause attached to the promise before it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the short passage about those who bring the truth and confirm it. The believers being addressed were a pressured minority in Mecca with a record they knew was uneven, and the surah alternates between severity and reassurance throughout. This ayah is the reassurance attached to the promise just made. The classical commentators report no particular occasion for it, and read it with the two ayat immediately before.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to cover or conceal; a farmer covering seed with soil uses the same verb. Forgiveness here is something placed over the deed rather than a declaration that the deed never happened.
A superlative rather than a plain adjective. Naming the worst as the thing covered implies the rest goes with it, since nothing is left standing above what has already been covered over.
The matching superlative on the other side of the exchange. It sets the rate of payment by a person's highest moment rather than by their average, which is the asymmetry the whole ayah is built on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Accounts in a trading town were settled by reckoning: goods weighed, debts set against credits, a balance struck at the end of a season. Everyone understood a ledger. They also understood that a creditor could choose to strike out an entry, and that a generous employer might pay a labourer at the rate of his best day's work rather than his ordinary one. Both gestures were known, and both were entirely discretionary.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for covering over in this ayah shares its root with the Quran's word for those who reject faith, which at its base means people who cover something up. The same action, concealment, is a fault in one direction and a mercy in the other, depending on who is doing the covering and what is being covered.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets out an economy that is unbalanced in the person's favour, and does so without pretending the deeds did not happen. What is described is covering, not denial, which keeps the moral record honest while removing its weight. Measuring reward by a person's best also implies that a life is read for what it was reaching toward rather than averaged out, which is a claim about how God reads a life rather than about how good the person was.

crossReferences.why: States almost the same exchange in the same terms, misdeeds remitted and reward set by the best.
Adds that the best of their deeds is accepted while their misdeeds are passed over entirely.
Goes a step further than covering, describing bad deeds exchanged outright for good ones.

studies.applyIt: Bring to mind the one thing you have done that you would least want read aloud. Do not argue with the feeling and do not go looking for others. Then read this ayah once with that specific thing in view, and notice that the promise is worded to cover exactly the worst item rather than the average one. That precision is the whole point.

studies.title: Is God Not Enough
studies.meaning: Two questions frame a pair of mirrored statements. The first asks whether God is not sufficient for His servant, and the occasion given for asking is intimidation: people were trying to frighten him with the powers they served. Then guidance and its loss are set out as exact opposites, each with no remedy available outside God. The second question closes the pair by naming God as mighty and as one who exacts what is owed. Commentators note that the word for sufficient appears here in a form used nowhere else.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The threats being answered were the ordinary ones of that town: warnings that offended powers would bring sickness, madness or ruin on a man who spoke against them. The commentators explain the intimidation as exactly this, the town's gods invoked as a danger to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) personally. The ayah does not argue with the threat. It answers with a question about who is sufficient.

keyTerms.note: An active participle from the verb to suffice. This exact form occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and it makes sufficiency a description of God rather than a report of what He happens to supply.
An intensive verb form, so repeated or sustained attempts to instil fear rather than one threat. The grammar makes the frightening something done at him over time, which fits a long campaign.
A phrase for one who exacts what is owed after a wrong. It is built as possession rather than as a verb, so it names a standing capacity rather than an act being carried out.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fear of an offended shrine was practical rather than abstract. People left vows and portions before a journey, and a man whose caravan failed or whose child sickened after slighting a sanctuary would hear about the connection from everyone he met. Threatening an opponent with the anger of a shrine was ordinary social pressure in that town, it cost the speaker nothing, and it was hard to answer.
studies.didYouKnow: The form of the word for sufficient used here occurs once in the Quran. Two ayat later the same idea returns in the first person, God suffices for me, in a phrase found in only one other place, the closing ayah of surah nine. Both times it is placed in a messenger's mouth as an answer to people turning away.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Sufficiency is put as a question rather than a claim, which leaves the answering to the hearer. The two mirrored sentences that follow refuse to make guidance a human achievement or its loss a human accident, while the surah elsewhere holds people fully answerable. Holding both together is characteristic: God's decision is final and the person is responsible, and neither statement is allowed to dissolve the other into a comfortable half-truth.

crossReferences.why: Closes another surah with the same first-person answer, God is enough for me, after people turn away.
States the same sufficiency as a plain promise: whoever relies on God, God suffices him.
Turns the question on the powers used to threaten, asking what they can lift or hold back.

studies.applyIt: Name the thing pressuring you right now: a person, a deadline, a figure in an account. Say what it is out loud in one plain sentence, without adjectives, because threats keep much of their force by staying vague. Then read the opening question of this ayah and answer it yourself, rather than letting the ayah answer it on your behalf.

studies.title: Can They Lift The Harm
studies.meaning: The argument opens with a concession the opponents supply themselves: asked who created the heavens and the earth, they answer God. From that admission the passage moves to a test with two directions. If God intends harm for me, can these lift it? If He intends mercy, can they hold it back? Neither question is answered, because neither needs an answer. The ayah then closes not with a conclusion but with a declaration of reliance, spoken in the first person.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The people addressed were not deniers of a creator; they acknowledged a supreme maker and used lesser powers as intermediaries, which is the position this surah has been dismantling since its opening ayat. The Quran returns to their admission several times in the Meccan surahs, always in the same form, a question put and an answer they cannot avoid giving. No specific occasion is reported here.

keyTerms.note: From a verb for uncovering, drawing back a cloth or a curtain. Harm is imagined as something laid over a person, so removing it means pulling the covering off rather than fighting it away.
From the verb for gripping and retaining. Paired with the previous word it makes the two questions exactly opposite in shape, one about taking away and one about keeping back.
A noun meaning what suffices, with a possessive ending, so literally my enough. The phrase occurs in only one other place in the Quran, at the close of the ninth surah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The shrines around Mecca were consulted for exactly these two purposes: to lift something that had already come, and to secure something wanted. Divining arrows were drawn before decisions, vows were made before a journey, and offerings were left in hope of rain or a safe return. The two questions in this ayah name the whole practical use of a shrine and ask whether either half of it works.
studies.didYouKnow: The admission this ayah opens with, that if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth they would say God, recurs in nearly identical wording at 29:61 and 31:25, and in shortened form at 43:87. In each place the answer is followed at once by a question about why they turn away, so the belief is treated as common ground.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the disagreement precisely. It is not about whether God exists or made the world, which the opponents grant, but about whether anything else has a share in running it. Reducing the question to two practical tests, lifting harm and withholding mercy, turns a doctrinal dispute into an operational one. The answer given is then not an argument at all but a stance: reliance, declared in the first person and left standing.

crossReferences.why: Records the same admission in nearly the same words, followed by praise and a note on their ignorance.
States the two directions as fact rather than question: none removes His harm, none repels His grace.
Asks the matching question about sufficiency two ayat earlier, answering the same intimidation.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you have quietly appointed as your backup: a savings figure, a contact, a qualification. It is probably worth having. Put the two questions of this ayah to it anyway, plainly and without drama. Can it lift what actually lands on you? Can it hold back what is sent? Then keep it, with its real size restored.

studies.title: Work From Where You Stand
studies.meaning: The instruction is a parting of ways rather than a threat. Each side is told to act from its own position, and the outcome is left to be discovered instead of argued. Commentators read the word for position as covering both a person's capacity and the ground they occupy, so the sentence means act as you are and from where you are. The second ayah completes it with what will become known, and that knowledge is described as arriving rather than as being demonstrated by anyone.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the later years when argument in the city had reached a stalemate and the message was meeting settled refusal rather than questions. The same formula appears in three other places in the Quran, always at the end of an exchange between a prophet and people who will not move, which suggests it belonged to a recognised way of closing a dispute. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A noun for the place a person occupies and the capacity that goes with it. It carries the physical sense of a station and the social sense of standing, so the instruction is to act as who you are.
An active participle rather than a verb, so it states a settled condition instead of an intention. The reply is not I will work but I am a worker, which declines the argument and simply carries on.
An active participle from the verb to stand or take up residence. Applied to suffering it means what has moved in and stays, rather than what passes through and is gone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Formal disputes in Arabia ended in recognised ways: a boast, an oath, or a challenge to wait and see whose fortune held. Rival poets closed an exchange with a line that left the verdict to time rather than to the audience. Saying carry on as you are and I will carry on as I am was a known move, understood by everyone present as ending a conversation rather than conceding it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase translated work according to your position appears four times in the Quran, here and at 6:135, 11:93 and 11:121. In every case it is spoken by a prophet to people who have refused him, and in every case what follows leaves the outcome to time rather than adding a further argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ending an argument is treated here as a legitimate move rather than as a failure. The passage assumes that some disagreements are not settled by better reasoning but by what happens, and it is willing to wait for that. It also puts both parties under the same instruction, which grants the opponents real agency. They are not being overpowered; they are left free to act, and the difference will show in the outcome rather than in the permission.

crossReferences.why: Closes another prophet's argument with the same formula, adding that both sides will now wait.
Uses the identical instruction and adds that the wrongdoers will not prevail in the end.
Reaches the same parting of ways in the shortest form the Quran gives it.

studies.applyIt: Identify one argument you keep restarting with someone who has already decided. Choose today to stop making the case and to put that energy into your own work instead. This is not giving up on the person. It is recognising that some disagreements are settled by what each of you does over years, and not by the next conversation.

studies.title: You Are Not Their Guardian
studies.meaning: Three clauses divide the responsibility. The Book was sent down for people and with truth; the benefit of taking it goes to whoever takes it; the loss of refusing falls on whoever refuses. Then the messenger is told plainly what he is not, an agent set over them. Commentators note that the word used is the ordinary one for someone entrusted with another person's affairs, so what is lifted here is a burden of custody rather than the duty to deliver the message at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is described repeatedly in this period as grieving over the refusal of his own people, and several passages from these years address that grief rather than the opponents. This ayah belongs to that group. The commentators read it together with the ayat just before it, which have told both sides to act from their own positions and leave the result alone.

keyTerms.note: The preposition carries weight. The Book is not only described as true but as accompanied by truth, sent with it, which the commentators take to cover the purpose and the manner of the sending too.
A preposition of benefit attached to the word for a person's self. The matching clause about straying uses a preposition of burden instead, so the grammar itself separates the gain from the cost.
The word for someone entrusted with another's affairs, who acts on their behalf and answers for the result. Denying it to the messenger removes liability for the outcome, not the duty to convey.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Trade in Mecca ran on agents. A merchant who could not travel appointed someone to carry his goods, sell them and return with the price, and that agent answered for what became of the consignment. The word used in this ayah is the ordinary commercial one. Telling the Prophet he was not their agent used a term the traders in his audience had signed themselves and understood exactly.
studies.didYouKnow: The word denied to the messenger here, an entrusted agent, is affirmed of God elsewhere in the Quran, and the phrase the excellent guardian is put in believers' mouths at 3:173. The same commercial term is thus withheld from the man delivering the message and applied to the one who sent it, within a single vocabulary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A line is drawn between conveying and controlling. Revelation is given for people, what they do with it belongs to them, and the one who brings it is not accountable for their choice. That protects the messenger from a grief he has no way to discharge, and it protects the reader from imagining that someone else's guidance is theirs to secure. Responsibility is individual on both sides of the exchange, and the ayah says so twice.

crossReferences.why: States the same limit directly: you are a reminder, and you have no control over them.
Asks whether he would compel people to believe when God has not willed it so.
Says plainly that their guidance is not his responsibility, since God guides whom He wills.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person whose choices you have been carrying as though they were your own account to settle. Say the second half of this ayah about them, using their name. You are not being told to stop caring or to stop speaking. You are being told which part of the outcome was never assigned to you, and invited to put that part down.

studies.title: Souls Taken In Sleep
studies.meaning: Two states are placed under a single verb. God receives souls at death, and receives those that have not died in their sleep; He then keeps the ones whose death is decreed and sends the others back until a named term. Commentators differ over what exactly is taken in sleep, some speaking of the soul itself and others of the faculty of awareness, and they record the range without settling it. What is not in dispute is the structure: a nightly departure, with a decision made each time about who returns.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, set inside a run of ayat arguing against powers that can neither harm nor help. Placing it here is deliberate: the argument moves from what other powers cannot do to something that happens to every listener every night. The surah is preoccupied throughout with death and the Day, and this is the ayah that brings both into the reader's own bed. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: From a root for receiving something complete, as a creditor takes the whole of what is owed. It is the Quran's usual verb for dying, and it frames death as a handing over rather than as an ending.
The noun for the time and place of sleeping, from the same root as the verb to sleep. Setting it beside death in one sentence makes the nightly event the smaller instance of the larger one.

A fixed period with a stated end, the same phrase used for the due date of a debt. Calling the term named implies it is already specified, and that the specifying was not done by the person living it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: People slept in the open, on roofs and in courtyards, through the hot months, and in a household sharing one room the difference between a sleeping body and a dead one was something everyone had had to check for at least once. Deaths in the night were common, particularly among the very young and the very old. The ayah does not argue that sleep resembles death; its audience had stood over someone at dawn not yet knowing which it was.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing sleep as a taking of the soul occurs only here in the Quran. One other passage, at 6:60, describes God taking people by night and raising them again by day using the same verb and ending with the same fixed term. Between them they are the whole of what the Quran says on the subject in these words.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes death continuous with something ordinary rather than setting it apart as an exception. If the soul is received every night and sent back, the last time is the same act without the return, which takes much of the strangeness out of dying without softening what it is. It also places the decision entirely on one side. What is offered to those who reflect is not a doctrine but the observation that they have been through this thousands of times already.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same nightly taking and raising, closing with the fixed term and the return.
Says death overtakes a person wherever they are, even inside fortified towers built to prevent it.
States the same fact in its barest form, mortality asserted of both parties in the argument.

studies.applyIt: Tonight, once you are lying down and beginning to lose the thread, notice the last moment you are aware of. You will not be able to notice the one after it, and nobody can. That edge is exactly what this ayah describes. Do not try to make anything of it or draw a lesson. Just find the edge once, and then sleep.

studies.title: All Intercession Belongs To God
studies.meaning: A question exposes the practice and a statement replaces it. They have taken intercessors besides God; the reply asks whether they would do so even if those intercessors own nothing at all and understand nothing. Then the correction arrives: intercession belongs entirely to God, along with the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, and the return is to Him. The commentators are careful here. The passage does not deny that intercession happens; it denies that anyone holds it independently of God's leave.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The people addressed described their objects of devotion in exactly these terms, as intercessors who would bring them nearer, and this surah quotes that claim in its third ayah. The commentators read the present pair as its direct answer. No specific occasion is reported for either. The wider argument of these years was not about whether God exists but about how access to Him is arranged.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to make a thing even by adding a second to it, the opposite of odd. An intercessor joins himself to your case, so the word pictures being paired with someone stronger rather than merely represented.
From the word for the tether used to hobble a camel. Reason is pictured as what holds a person's judgement in place, so lacking it means having nothing to keep the mind from wandering off.
Definite, and made the predicate of a phrase meaning belonging to God, which is the strongest construction Arabic has for saying that the whole of a thing is His and none of it is held elsewhere.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Access in Arabia ran through patrons. A stranger entering a town needed a protector to speak for him, a debtor needed someone to stand between himself and a creditor, and a man in danger sought the protection of a chief whose name would make enemies reconsider. The whole system worked because the patron had power of his own, and the reply here goes straight at that assumption: these hold nothing.
studies.didYouKnow: The claim being answered is quoted earlier in this same surah, at its third ayah, where those addressed say they serve lesser powers only so that these may bring them nearer to God. The answer is held back for forty ayat and then given in two sentences, one dismantling the assumption and one stating where intercession actually rests.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not abolish intercession; it relocates the ownership of it. Saying that all of it belongs to God makes any intercession that happens an expression of His will rather than a lever upon it, which keeps hope intact while removing the idea of an independent channel. Placed beside the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, it also implies that having power and having the right to intercede are finally the same question.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the claim this pair answers, that lesser powers are served only to bring people nearer to God.
States the same limit inside the Throne Verse: no one intercedes with Him except by His leave.
Records the identical phrase, these are our intercessors with God, and answers it on the spot.

studies.applyIt: Notice, this week, the moment when you ask someone to put in a word for you. There is nothing wrong with it; human institutions run that way. Just watch what happens in your chest at the moment of asking, and compare it with what happens when you ask God directly, with no one in between. The difference in that feeling is the subject here.

studies.title: When God Alone Is Mentioned
studies.meaning: The reaction described is not an intellectual one. When God is mentioned by Himself, without the others, the hearts of those who do not believe in the hereafter contract with distaste; when the others are named, the same people brighten. The word for the first reaction is strong and physical. Commentators locate the offence precisely in the word alone: nothing objectionable has been said about God, only that He has been named without company, and that is what produces the recoil.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Devotion in the town was plural by habit, and a public statement naming God by Himself excluded a whole apparatus of shrines, guardianship and seasonal trade on which many families depended. The commentators describe the reaction as social as much as theological. No specific occasion is reported. The ayah sits inside a run about intercession and works as its emotional counterpart.

keyTerms.note: An emphatic word for singleness placed after the name. The whole reaction in the ayah depends on it: the offence lies not in the mention but in the absence of anyone mentioned alongside.
A rare five-consonant verb for a body contracting in disgust. It occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and it names a reaction of the stomach rather than of the mind or the argument.
The root behind it covers good news and the outer surface of the skin alike, so the word names news showing on a face. It is set deliberately against the contraction in the first half.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's standing rested on a sanctuary that housed many objects of devotion and drew pilgrims from across the peninsula at fixed seasons. Naming God alone was not only a religious statement; it touched the arrangements of an entire town, its guardianship offices, its truce months and its markets. People heard the exclusion in it immediately, well before they had considered whether the claim was true.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing the recoil occurs once in the whole Quran. It belongs to a rare five-consonant pattern that Arabic keeps for vivid physical reactions. The word for the opposite response, in the same ayah, comes from a root that also gives the ordinary word for skin, so both halves of the contrast are described as things happening to a body.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Resistance to God is diagnosed here as an aversion rather than a conclusion, and it is tied specifically to disbelief in a life after this one. That link repays attention: if there is no reckoning, exclusive devotion costs a great deal and returns nothing visible. The passage therefore treats doctrine and appetite as connected, and admits that the argument it is having is partly with what people want to be true.

crossReferences.why: Reports the same reaction, backs turned in aversion when the Lord is mentioned alone in the recitation.
Explains the same refusal from the other side: when God alone was called on, you disbelieved.
Sets out the position that makes an exclusive mention feel like a loss to the people addressed.

studies.applyIt: Watch for the small flinch. Sometime this week you will hear something true, correctly said, and still not want it, and the reason will be what accepting it would cost you rather than anything about the claim. Catch yourself once. Do not argue with the flinch and do not obey it. Just note that you had one, and carry on with your day.

studies.title: You Will Judge Between Them
studies.meaning: A prayer is given to be said, and its shape is the instruction. It opens with a vocative form of the divine name used only a handful of times in the Quran, then names God twice by what He does: opening the heavens and the earth into being, and knowing both the hidden and the seen. Only after that does the content arrive, and it is not a request for victory. It is an acknowledgement that God will judge between His servants in what they differed about, and it stops there.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and placed at a point where the surah has finished arguing. The dispute in the city was not going to be settled by evidence, since both sides had heard everything the other had. The commentators read the ayah as instruction in what to do when an argument has run out, and note that what is asked for is a judgement rather than a punishment. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A special vocative form of the divine name, ending in a doubled consonant that replaces the usual particle for calling. It occurs five times in the Quran, and in each place it stands at the head of a prayer.

From a verb meaning to split something open, used of a seed breaking and of a fast being broken. Creation is pictured as something opened rather than assembled, and one surah takes its title from this word.
Two opposites named to cover everything between them. The second is the ordinary word for giving testimony, so the pair takes in what nobody saw and what everybody did.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: When a dispute could not be settled inside a tribe, both parties went to an arbitrator whose standing they both accepted, and the point of him was that he knew things neither side could hide. Arbitration failed when no such person could be agreed on. In a town where the two sides had run out of common ground, a prayer naming God as the one who judges was a recognisable legal move, made upward.
studies.didYouKnow: The vocative form that opens this prayer occurs five times in the Quran: at 3:26, 5:114, 8:32, 10:10 and here. The name used next for God, the one who splits things open in creating them, occurs six times in the Book and gives the thirty-fifth surah its title.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer models something specific: what to say when you are sure you are right and the argument is over. It does not ask for the opponent's defeat and it does not ask for vindication now. It names God's knowledge of the hidden, which is precisely the thing neither party in a human dispute can supply, and then leaves the verdict where it belongs. Restraint is built into the form of the words.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the same rare vocative, before a statement about sovereignty given and taken away.
Puts the same request in almost the same words: our Lord will gather us, then judge between us.
Ends a parallel argument the same way, with God gathering both sides and the return being to Him.

studies.applyIt: Take one dispute where you are sure you are right and the other person will not move. Instead of rehearsing your case again tonight, say this prayer's shape in your own words: name God, name what He knows that you do not, and then hand over the verdict rather than the person. Notice afterwards whether anything in your shoulders has changed.

studies.title: Everything On Earth, Twice Over
studies.meaning: A hypothetical is built to be impossible and is then made useless. If the wrongdoers owned all that is on the earth, and as much again beside it, they would spend the whole of it to buy their way out. The ayah does not say the offer is refused. It says something else appears to them from God that they had never reckoned with. Commentators note the shift: a scene of bargaining is set up and then replaced by a scene of arrival, which unsettles more than a refusal would.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a merchant city whose leading families measured standing in caravan shares and stored goods. Ransom was a familiar transaction there: captives were bought back after raids at negotiated rates, and everyone knew roughly what a life cost. The ayah takes that ordinary arithmetic and extends it past any figure that could exist. No specific occasion is reported for it.

keyTerms.note: A doubling clause that adds an equal quantity to an amount already total. Since the first amount was everything on earth, the second cannot exist, and that impossibility is the point being made.
The verb for buying a captive's release, an ordinary transaction after a raid. It assumes a seller willing to deal, and the rest of the ayah quietly removes that assumption without announcing it.
An accounting verb for calculating what is owed and expected. What appears is described as outside their reckoning, so the failure named is one of estimation rather than of information.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: After a raid, captives were held and then ransomed, and the negotiation was public and precise: so many camels for a fighting man, fewer for a boy. Families sold property to raise the sum, and some could not raise it at all. Everyone in that audience had paid such a price, watched one argued over, or known a household that failed to meet one. The ayah speaks the language of a transaction they had all seen conducted.
studies.didYouKnow: The hypothetical in this ayah, everything on earth and the like of it besides, appears in one other place in the Quran, at 13:18, where it also concerns people who did not answer their Lord. The verb used for the attempted ransom is the ordinary commercial one for buying back a captive, not a specialised religious term.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Wealth is not condemned here so much as measured. Setting the sum at everything that exists and then doubling it establishes that quantity was never the relevant variable, and it does so without saying property is worthless. The ending carries the more serious claim. What appears is described as entirely outside their calculation, which suggests the deepest failure was not in what they owned but in what they thought the situation was.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical hypothetical, everything on earth and its like, of those who did not answer their Lord.
States the refusal concretely: an earth's fill of gold would not be accepted as ransom from them.
The next ayah completes the scene by naming what appears to them: their own deeds and their own mockery.

studies.applyIt: Work out, roughly, the number you have privately decided would make you safe. Most people have one even if they have never said it aloud. Write it down and look at it for a moment. This ayah is not telling you the figure is wrong. It is asking whether safety is the kind of thing that has a price, and leaving you to answer.

studies.title: Surrounded By What They Mocked
studies.meaning: Two things appear and one closes in. The bad of what they earned becomes visible, and then what they used to ridicule surrounds them. Nothing new is introduced into the scene: the material of the reckoning is the person's own record and the person's own jokes. Commentators note that the passage names ridicule specifically, not rejection in general, as the thing that returns, and that the verb for surrounding is one the Quran reserves almost entirely for what a person set in motion coming back.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Mockery rather than argument was the main instrument used against the message in this period: opponents gave the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) nicknames, imitated the recitation, and made the raising of the dead a subject for jokes at gatherings. Several Meccan passages answer laughter rather than reasoning, and this is one of them. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A plural from the word for what is bad or ugly to look at. Paired here with a verb for becoming visible, it treats wrongs as things already present and simply not yet in view.
A verb for closing in from every side. The Quran uses it almost only of something a person started coming back around them, so the word itself makes the outcome a return rather than an addition.
A verb form implying seeking amusement at something, so mockery as entertainment rather than as insult. The tense makes it a settled habit rather than a single incident anyone could regret.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation in Arabia was made and unmade in verse. A satirical poem could travel between markets and follow a family for generations, and the standard weapon against a new claim was not refutation but ridicule delivered well enough to be repeated. Making someone laughable was a recognised political act. Answering mockery was harder than answering argument, because there was nothing in it to take hold of.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence about being surrounded by what they used to ridicule occurs six times in the Quran, at 11:8, 16:34, 40:83, 45:33, 46:26 and here. It is among the most repeated full clauses in the Book, and one of those occurrences stands in the surah that immediately follows this one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reckoning described contains nothing imported. It is made of a person's own deeds becoming visible and their own mockery closing in, which presents judgement as disclosure rather than as an addition from outside. That has a consequence for the present: if nothing new is added later, then what will be seen then is being assembled now. Ridicule is singled out because it is the cheapest available way to avoid a question.

crossReferences.why: States the same return of mockery, there of messengers who were ridiculed before this one.
Repeats the identical clause: evils becoming visible, and the mocked thing closing in around them.
The ayah before, where what appears to them from God is what they had never reckoned with.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you make jokes about that you have never actually examined. Most people have one, and the joke is usually load-bearing. You do not have to stop making it. Just once, ask what you would have to look at if the joke were unavailable to you, and then decide for yourself whether you want to look.

studies.title: I Earned This By Knowing
studies.meaning: What is quoted here is not forgetfulness but a theory. Harm comes, the man calls; relief arrives, and he explains it, saying he was given it because of what he knows. The explanation is what the passage is after. It is then reclassified twice in a single breath: the favour was a test, and the sentence has been said before by people whose earnings did not save them. Commentators note that the man is not denying God so much as inserting himself as the cause.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience included successful traders who could point to real skill behind their success: routes learned, seasons judged, partners chosen well. The claim in the ayah would not have sounded absurd to them, which is why it is quoted rather than argued with. The same sentence is put in the mouth of a wealthy figure of an earlier generation elsewhere in the Quran. No specific occasion is reported here.

keyTerms.note: A verb for handing over the use of something without transferring ownership, as an owner puts property in a manager's hands. The word itself already answers the claim the man is about to make.
The preposition means resting on or by virtue of, so the knowledge is being named as the ground of the gift. It is a claim about causation, not merely a boast about competence.
From a root for putting metal in fire to separate it from its ore. A test in this sense is not a puzzle to be solved but heat applied to show what a thing actually is.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A Meccan merchant's skill was real and measurable. He knew which passes were safe in which month, what a load of hides fetched in Syria against what it cost at home, and which families honoured their debts. Fortunes were visibly made by judgement rather than luck. In that setting, crediting your own knowledge for your prosperity was the natural reading of the evidence, and everyone did it.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence quoted in this ayah, that he was given it on account of knowledge, occurs in exactly one other place in the Quran, at 28:78, where it is spoken by an enormously wealthy man of Moses' generation just before the earth swallows his house. The wording is identical, which links the anonymous man here to a named cautionary figure.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not attack competence or deny that skill produces results. What it targets is the move from having a cause to being the cause. Calling the favour a test also changes its meaning without changing its contents: the same wealth is either evidence of standing or an examination in progress, and nothing observable settles which. That leaves the reader with a question about interpretation rather than a claim about wealth.

crossReferences.why: Puts the identical sentence in the mouth of a wealthy man and follows it with the collapse of his house.
States the opposite reading plainly: whatever favour you have is from God, and you cry to Him in harm.
Describes the same reversal earlier in this surah, where the prayer itself is what gets forgotten.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing that has gone well for you recently and write down the honest chain of causes, including your own effort, in order. Then keep going past the last item you controlled. Everyone's chain has a point where it stops being yours. Find where yours is, name it accurately, and leave the rest of the list standing as it is.

studies.title: It Caught Up With Them
studies.meaning: The sentence turns on a change of tense. What earlier peoples earned struck them, past and finished; what the wrongdoers among the present audience earn will strike them, stated as a future with no condition attached. Between the two halves the passage names the group being addressed with a demonstrative, these ones here, which brings the history into the room. The last clause closes the exit: they are not people who can render anything powerless or slip out of reach.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just quoted a sentence spoken by earlier generations and pointed out that what they earned did not help them. This ayah completes that movement by turning the history on the listeners. The commentators read the demonstrative as pointing at the specific opponents in the city rather than at people in general. No particular occasion is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A verb used of a disaster landing on someone, and of an arrow finding its target. It implies accuracy rather than randomness, which is why translations reach for words like befell or caught up with.
A demonstrative for what is close at hand, used of people present rather than absent. Its effect is to move the argument from a story about the past to a remark about the room.
From a verb meaning to render someone unable, so it covers both outrunning a pursuer and frustrating an attempt. The negation denies them both possibilities in a single word.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debt in a trading town was enforced socially. A man who could not pay might be given time, but he could not simply move away: the routes were few, the towns were connected by kin, and a name travelled faster than a caravan. The idea of an obligation catching up with someone was not a metaphor for that audience. It described how their economy actually worked.
studies.didYouKnow: The word denying them any escape occurs seven times in the Quran, always in the negative and always of people who assume distance or delay will protect them. In this ayah it is the last word of the sentence, so the passage closes on the removal of the exit rather than on the arrival of the consequence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Consequence is presented here as continuous rather than as an intervention. The same clause is used of a vanished generation and of a living audience, with only the tense changed, which quietly asserts that one moral order covers both. It also refuses the two comforts people actually rely on, that the past was different and that they personally will be the exception, and it names the second of these directly.

crossReferences.why: The ayah before it, where what earlier generations earned availed them nothing when it came.
Uses the same word to deny escape, saying they cannot frustrate God on earth or in the heaven.
States that the pattern of earlier generations does not change, and no one alters God's way.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you are relying on time to sort something out for you: an unanswered message, a bill, a conversation you owe someone. Time is genuinely a healer for some things and a compounder for others. Sort one item from your list into the right column today, honestly, and then act on that single item rather than on the list.

studies.title: Spread Wide Or Measured Out
studies.meaning: Two verbs are set against each other: God spreads provision out for whom He wills, and He measures it. The second verb does not mean withholding out of poverty; it means setting an amount. Placed immediately after a man crediting his own knowledge for his wealth, the sentence removes the assumption underneath that claim, that provision tracks merit. What is offered at the end is not a consolation but a category: this is among the signs, and the people who read it as one are named as those who believe.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following directly on the quoted boast about knowledge and the reminder that earlier people said the same. The surah is speaking to a town where fortunes were visibly unequal and where the leading families read their own prosperity as evidence of favour. The commentators connect the ayat closely. No specific occasion is reported for this one, and its formula recurs in several other surahs of the same period.

keyTerms.note: The verb for unrolling a cloth or opening the hand flat. Provision is pictured as something laid out to its full width rather than counted, which is why the opposite verb is about measure and not about refusal.

From the root for capacity and determination, the same one behind the word for decree. Applied to provision it means setting an exact amount, so restriction here is a calculation rather than a withdrawal.

Everything a creature is given to live on, not only money: food, health, time, family. The word covers the whole supply, which is why a narrow reading of this ayah as being about income misses most of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Mecca was strikingly uneven and its causes were visible. A family with a share in the winter and summer caravans could prosper for generations while a client family a street away stayed poor with the same hours of work. Everyone knew who had a stake and who did not. The claim that the distribution was decided elsewhere was heard by people who could see how much of it they had not chosen.
studies.didYouKnow: This exact formula, that God spreads the provision for whom He wills and measures it, appears in nine places in the Quran. In several of them it is attached to a warning: at 42:27 it comes with the observation that if God expanded provision for all His servants without measure, they would grow oppressive on the earth.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah severs the link between provision and worth in both directions, which protects two different readers. It denies the wealthy the inference that having more means being favoured, and it denies the poor the inference that having less means being rejected. Naming the arrangement a sign then asks for something harder than acceptance: it asks that the distribution be read rather than merely endured or enjoyed.

crossReferences.why: Gives a reason for the measure: unlimited provision would make people transgress on the earth.
Shows people learning this lesson the day after envying a rich man whose house was swallowed.
Says God apportions livelihood among people and raises some above others in rank.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you know who has clearly been given more than you in one specific area, and someone who has clearly been given less. Hold all three of you in mind at once for a moment, without ranking anyone. That is what this ayah is asking you to look at. Then get on with your day, which is the other half of it.

studies.title: Do Not Despair Of Mercy
studies.meaning: The address does its work before any argument starts. People who have squandered themselves are still called God's servants. The bond is stated before the problem is named. Then despair is ruled out, and the reason given carries no small print at all: God forgives wrongs, all of them. Early scholars read this ayah with the two that follow, which call for turning back. So the openness described is the ground for trying to return, not a replacement for it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical sources report that this answered the fear of people who had committed grave wrongs before Islam and believed no turning back would be accepted from them. Several accounts are preserved and they differ over which individuals are meant. In the surah it arrives inside a warning about consequences catching up with people, so the opening is placed in the middle of the thing being warned about.

keyTerms.note: The word for running through property wastefully. Applying it to what someone does to their own soul borrows a picture from inheritance law: capital spent, with nothing to show for it.
A severe word for hope abandoned rather than merely low, used of someone who has stopped expecting anything at all. It is the state being forbidden here, not the wrongdoing that produced it.

A single word making the preceding noun completely general. It is what removes the category of exception a reader would otherwise supply, and it is placed after the word for wrongs rather than before.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The word for excess belonged to the vocabulary of property. A man who ran through an inheritance was described with it, and he could lose his standing and the management of his own affairs to relatives who stepped in. Families knew such a man and spoke about him. Using that word for what a person does to their own soul put a familiar domestic figure into the sentence.
studies.didYouKnow: A number of classical scholars record this as the most hopeful ayah in the Quran. They report that description as a verdict already in circulation, rather than offering it themselves. What sets the ayah apart is in the grammar of the sentence, not in its style. One short word makes the term for wrongs completely general. No exception is named anywhere in the sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two claims are made together. Forgiveness is stated with no limit on its reach. And despair is named as the thing to guard against, not as a fitting answer to serious wrongdoing. That turns an instinct around. The person who feels their own case is unique is told that the sense of being unique is itself the danger. The word used to address them settles the point before the argument reaches it.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same prohibition in a father's mouth after years of loss, and names who does despair.
Has Abraham ask the question directly, who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except those astray.
Supplies what the early scholars read alongside this, the instruction to turn back before the time runs out.

studies.applyIt: Write down, privately, the one thing you assume is past forgiving. Then read this ayah once, slowly, with that written in front of you. Notice which of the two you find easier to believe. You do not have to resolve anything today. The ayah's argument works on despair rather than on the wrong, and despair is the part still in your hands.
studies.explainEasier: God calls people who have hurt themselves by doing wrong his servants. He tells them not to give up hope in his mercy. God forgives every sin. He is the one who forgives and is gentle.

studies.title: Turn Before It Comes
studies.meaning: Three instructions arrive in two ayat, each carrying the same deadline. Turn back to your Lord, submit to Him, and follow the best of what was sent down to you, and do all of it before something arrives that cannot be negotiated with. Commentators explain the best of what was sent down as the commands within the Book rather than a ranking of its verses, since the Book also records what people said and did. The urgency is carried entirely by the repeated clause.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following immediately on the announcement that God forgives all sins. The commentators read this pair as the practical half of that announcement: the ayah before removes despair, and these two say what to do with the room it opens. The people addressed were being spoken to as those who still had time and had no way of knowing how much. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A verb for returning to a place you belong to, used of a man coming home and of water finding its channel again. It implies a known route rather than a new direction being struck out in.
A superlative from a root that carries beauty and goodness together. Commentators take the phrase it heads as the commands within the Book, rather than as a ranking of some verses above others.
An adverb for what arrives with no approach, used of a guest at the door and of death. It rules out the assumption that there will be signs to read in good time.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Caravans left on fixed days and did not wait for anyone. A trader who had not settled his affairs by departure watched the animals go and lost a season. Truce months ended on known dates, after which the roads became dangerous again. That audience organised its life around deadlines no argument could shift, and the phrase before it comes upon you would have sounded to them like ordinary practical advice.
studies.didYouKnow: Each instruction in this passage is attached to the same clause, before the punishment comes upon you, and the second time it is expanded with a word meaning suddenly. What follows immediately is a set of quoted regrets: three sentences a person might say afterwards, each beginning in the same grammatical way, so the commands and the regrets form one designed unit.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing these instructions directly after a promise of total forgiveness fixes the relation between the two. Mercy is announced first and without conditions, and only then is something asked, which makes the asking a response to generosity rather than its price. The deadline is real and its timing is withheld, so the passage produces urgency without producing a schedule, and leaves nobody able to calculate a safe latest moment.

crossReferences.why: The announcement these commands follow, that God forgives all sins and despair of His mercy is refused.
Marks where turning back stops being accepted, at the moment death is already arriving.
Gives the regret of someone asking for a short delay to do what this passage asks now.

studies.applyIt: Choose the smallest thing you have been meaning to put right with God and do it within the next hour, not tonight and not tomorrow. A prayer prayed properly rather than quickly, a debt of thanks paid, one sentence of apology sent. The whole force of the passage sits in the word before, and an hour is short enough to count as a real deadline.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Alas For What I Neglected
studies.meaning: A voice is quoted before it has ever spoken. The commands just given are given so that no soul should have to say this, and the sentence has two halves: regret over what was let slip in relation to God, and an admission of having been one of the scoffers. Commentators discuss the phrase rendered as the side of God, taking it as His claim, His nearness, or simply the matter of Him, and they preserve the range. All read the regret as being over neglect rather than over any act.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has spent its length addressing people who treated the message as something to laugh at, and this is the point where it lets one of them speak, years ahead of the moment. The commentators note that the quotation is placed before the event so that it can be used, which makes it a warning rather than a report. No specific occasion is given.

keyTerms.note: A vocative addressed to one's own grief, calling regret by name as though it were a person standing there. The form occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and it is the sound of someone speaking to himself.
An intensive verb for letting something slip through carelessness rather than by decision. It names an omission, which is why the regret in this ayah is not about a deed done but about a matter left.
The ordinary word for a person's side. Used here of God it puzzled the commentators, who read it variously as His claim, His nearness, or the matter of Him, and preserved all three.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Regret in that culture was performed aloud. Mourners cried set phrases, and a man who had lost a fortune or a son said so in words the whole quarter recognised and expected. Grief was not a private arrangement. Quoting a phrase of self-address in this form put the future speaker in a posture everyone had watched: a person in the open, naming his own loss to nobody in particular.
studies.didYouKnow: The exclamation in this ayah occurs once in the Quran and is grammatically odd: it uses the form for calling out to a person, but the one called is the speaker's own regret. The phrase rendered as the side of God is also unique to this ayah, which is why the classical commentaries record several readings of it instead of settling on one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The regret quoted is not for a crime but for a shortfall, which changes what is being warned about. It is possible to arrive at the end having done nothing dramatic and still have this sentence to say. The pairing with mockery is exact as well: scoffing is named as the mechanism by which the neglect was sustained, since a thing you are able to laugh at is a thing you never have to schedule.

crossReferences.why: Puts almost the same words in their mouths, alas for our neglect, when the Hour arrives suddenly.
Shows the same regret as an action, a man biting his hands over the way he did not take.
The ayah before, whose whole stated purpose is that this sentence should never have to be said.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you are currently letting slide rather than refusing outright. Not a sin you are wrestling with, but something you keep meaning to get to. Write it on paper, in four words. The regret quoted here is about exactly that category, and the smallest useful response is to give one of those items a time this week.

studies.title: Three Excuses And One Answer
studies.meaning: Two more sentences are quoted in advance, each offered as an alternative to the first. One moves the blame upward: had God guided me, I would have been among the careful. The other asks for a repeat, one more turn and I would do well. The answer then arrives with no preamble, and it is not a refutation but a record. My signs came to you; you called them lies, you made yourself great, and you were among those who refused. Commentators note that the reply answers the second request by describing the first opportunity.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The two excuses match arguments actually in circulation in the city: that guidance had not been given, and that any reckoning was too remote to act on. The surah has been answering the first throughout by insisting both on God's decision and on human responsibility, without letting either cancel the other. The three quoted sentences form one sequence with the ayah before them. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A noun for one repetition of a movement, from a verb used of a horseman wheeling around to charge again. It asks for a second run at the same course rather than for pardon of the first.
A particle used only to contradict a negative statement, so it cannot open a sentence at random. Its presence shows the excuse just made was heard as a denial, and is being reversed.
A verb form meaning to seek greatness for oneself or reckon oneself great. It describes something done rather than a temperament held, which matters because the reply is listing actions.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A rider who lost an engagement could ask for another pass, and a merchant who misjudged a season could take out a second consignment. Almost every failure in that world was repeatable, which is how both the economy and the fighting worked. The request for one more turn was therefore not fanciful to that audience. It was the most natural thing a person in trouble would think to ask for.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for another chance occurs three times in the Quran in this sense, at 2:167, 26:102 and in this ayah. In every one of them it is spoken by people after the outcome has already become visible to them, and in none of the three is it granted.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply refuses both moves at once. To the claim that guidance was withheld it answers with a delivery record, which does not settle the deep question of decree but does close the excuse. To the request for another attempt it answers with an account of the first one. Between them the passage holds the line the whole surah holds: God's will is sovereign, and a person's own record is still theirs to answer for.

crossReferences.why: Records the same request to be sent back, made by people standing in view of the Fire.
Puts the same plea in the mouths of the guilty, who say they have now seen and heard.
The first of the three quoted regrets, of which these two sentences are the alternatives.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself the next time you explain a failure by something outside you. The explanation may even be true. Add one sentence to it anyway, naming the part that was yours, and say both together. The passage answers an excuse not by denying the circumstances but by putting the record beside them, which is a thing you can practise in miniature.

studies.title: Faces Darkened On That Day
studies.meaning: One image and one question. Those who told lies about God are seen with their faces darkened, and then the question asks whether there is not room in Hell for the arrogant. The connection between the halves is the whole point: inventing about God is treated as an act of arrogance rather than as an error of understanding. Commentators note the passive form of the darkening, something done to the face rather than an expression it takes on, and read it against the ayat about faces made bright on the same day.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the sequence of quoted excuses with an image instead of another reply. The people in view are those who attributed statements, prohibitions and permissions to God without warrant, which was a live practice in the city, since customary rules were commonly given divine authority. The commentators connect the ayah to that charge specifically rather than to disbelief in general. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A passive form built from the word for black. It describes a change worked on a face rather than a look someone adopts, which is why the same word covers an ordinary face falling at bad news.
A form meaning those who make themselves great, from the root for bigness. It names a claim being asserted rather than a feeling held, which is what ties it to speaking on God's behalf.
From a verb for staying somewhere, the ordinary word for where a traveller puts up. The plainness is deliberate: it makes the destination a residence rather than a spectacle.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A face was read in public. Business was done in the open, disputes were settled in front of witnesses, and a man's standing shifted the moment his expression did in front of others. The Arabic idiom for a face going dark was in ordinary use for humiliation and for grief, and it named something the whole gathering could see at once, before a word had been said.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact expression for a darkened face occurs three times in the Quran. In the two other places, at 16:58 and 43:17, it describes a man's face on being told his newborn is a girl, a reaction the Quran presents as shameful. The same words are then used here of people who invented statements about God.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A specific wrong is identified and given a specific weight. Inventing about God is not treated as an intellectual mistake but as the arrogance of speaking with an authority nobody granted, which is why the sentence about the arrogant follows immediately. The reversal is exact: the person who claimed to speak for the highest is shown at the lowest, and what is named first is not pain but exposure.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the same day as faces whitened and faces blackened, with the two put side by side.
Uses the identical phrase for a darkened face, of a man ashamed at the birth of a daughter.
Names the same wrong earlier in this surah: who is more wrong than one who lies about God.

studies.applyIt: Notice this week when you are tempted to add authority to an opinion you already hold, by saying that religion requires it or that God wants it. Say the opinion without the borrowed weight and see whether it still stands. If it does, you have lost nothing. If it does not, you have learned something worth knowing about it.

studies.title: Saved To Their Place Of Safety
studies.meaning: The rescue is described with an unusual noun: God delivers the mindful by, or to, their place of triumph, and the Arabic carries both readings, which the commentators record without choosing. Then two negatives, no harm touching them and no grief, and then two statements about God that appear to change the subject and do not. He is the creator of everything, and the one in charge of everything. The safety just promised is being grounded in the reach of the one promising it, stated as total twice in a single line.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a community with no protector powerful enough to matter. Clan protection was the ordinary security of that world, and several of the believers had lost theirs or had never held any. Setting a promise of deliverance beside a statement that God manages everything answers a practical anxiety rather than a theoretical one. The commentators report no specific occasion for either ayah.

keyTerms.note: A noun of place from the verb to succeed or to escape. It occurs three times in the Quran and can mean the safety reached or the reason for reaching it, and commentators keep both senses open.
A verb for sorrow over what is past or lost, distinct from the fear that looks forward. Paired here with harm, it covers both directions of time, leaving nothing to dread and nothing to mourn.
The same commercial word this surah earlier denied to the messenger, affirmed here of God without limit. What one man is told he is not, God is said to be over every single thing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Safety in Arabia was a matter of belonging. A man travelled under the protection of a clan, and if that protection lapsed he could be killed on the road with no consequence to anyone. Some of the earliest believers had their protection publicly withdrawn by their own families and had to arrange substitutes. To people in that position, a promise of being brought through to safety was not an abstraction.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the place of triumph in this ayah occurs three times in the Quran, here and at 3:188 and 78:31. At 3:188 it names an escape people wrongly imagine they have secured; at 78:31 it names the triumph waiting for the mindful. This is the only one of the three where the word is attached to the act of being brought through.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Deliverance and sovereignty are stated in one breath, and that is the argument rather than a change of subject. A promise of safety is only as good as the reach of whoever makes it, and the reach here is given twice as everything, once in creating and once in managing. The two negatives deserve attention as well: what is promised first is not pleasure but the absence of harm and of grief.

crossReferences.why: Closes with the same pair, no fear upon them and no grief, of whoever submits and does good.
Has angels say those same two words, do not fear and do not grieve, to people who stood firm.
Denies the messenger the very word affirmed of God here, one placed in charge of others.

studies.applyIt: Write down the two things you are most afraid of and the two you are most sorry about. Four lines, no explanations. This ayah promises the removal of exactly those two categories and nothing else in its first clause. Read it once with your four lines in front of you, and notice that the promise is narrower and more specific than you expected.

studies.title: The Keys Of The Heavens
studies.meaning: An image, and then a question with its sting at the end. To God belong the keys of the heavens and the earth, and those who reject His signs are the ones who come out short. Then the messenger is told to ask whether it is something other than God they are instructing him to serve, and the address closes by naming them ignorant. Commentators note the rare word for keys and read the two ayat together, so that the argument turns on knowledge: the people issuing instructions are the ones who do not know.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Pressure on the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in this period included proposals from the city's leaders, some of them offering arrangements in which each side would show respect to the other's objects of devotion. The commentators read this instruction as a refusal of that kind of offer. The reply is framed as a question rather than a statement, and no further occasion is reported for it.

keyTerms.note: A rare plural that classical lexicographers gloss as keys and as the means of control. It occurs in only one other place in the Quran, and in both it is followed by the heavens and the earth.
A commercial term for those whose trade has come out short. It measures an outcome rather than naming a fault, so the word assesses the transaction a person made rather than insulting them.
In Arabic usage this covers not knowing and behaving rashly together, and its opposite is forbearance as much as learning. The word charges the speakers with recklessness as well as with error.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Keys were serious objects in that world. Custody of the key to the sanctuary at Mecca was a hereditary office held by one family, and it carried standing across the peninsula. Storerooms, treasuries and city gates worked the same way: whoever held the key held the thing itself. An audience hearing that the keys of the heavens and the earth belonged to God knew exactly what size of claim was being made.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for keys in this ayah occurs twice in the Quran, here and at 42:12, and in both places it is followed immediately by the heavens and the earth. At 42:12 the sentence goes on to provision spread out and measured; here it turns instead to those who reject the signs, so the same image opens onto two different arguments.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Holding the keys is a claim about access as much as about ownership, since whoever holds them decides what opens. Set beside the question that follows, the passage argues that instructing someone to serve another power is not only wrong but uninformed, a proposal made by people who do not know who holds what. Calling the objection ignorance rather than wickedness is a deliberate choice, and it leaves a door open.

crossReferences.why: The only other place this word for keys appears, followed there by provision spread out and measured.
Says the keys of the unseen are with Him alone, and that none knows them but He.
Answers the same kind of proposal, a mutual exchange of worship, with a flat refusal.

studies.applyIt: Think of a piece of advice you have been given recently by someone confident and poorly informed. You probably did not take it, and you probably were not rude about it either. Notice how that felt from the inside. This ayah is teaching a way of refusing that names the problem as not knowing, and leaves the person their dignity.

studies.title: Worship God And Be Thankful
studies.meaning: A warning is reported as having been revealed to this messenger and to those before him in the same terms: associating anything with God would empty his work and leave him among those who come out short. The severity lies in who is being addressed. Then the correction arrives as two short commands, serve God and be among the thankful, and the second is not an ornament. Commentators note that gratitude is named as the alternative to association, which makes the whole argument turn on acknowledgement rather than on ritual.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following directly on the demand that he serve something besides God. The commentators read these two ayat as the answer to that demand, delivered not as an argument but as a report of what he had already been told. Saying the same warning was given to the messengers before him places the refusal inside a line of practice rather than in one man's temperament. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: From a verb used of an animal that has eaten something poisonous and swells until it dies. Work is pictured swelling with nothing inside it, which is why the English word vain fits better than cancelled.
From the word for a business partner holding a share. The image is commercial: giving another a stake in what belongs to one owner entirely, which is why the loss is then described in trading terms.
From a root whose basic sense is a fullness that shows, used of an animal heavy with milk. Thankfulness in Arabic is therefore something visible from outside rather than an inward state kept private.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Partnerships ran Meccan trade. Two or three men put up shares in a consignment and divided the return in proportion, and the arrangements were precise because everything depended on them holding. Adding a partner to a venture without the owner's agreement was a recognised wrong with a name and a remedy. The vocabulary of association in this ayah comes straight from that world and was heard as commercial language.
studies.didYouKnow: The warning here is addressed to the messenger himself and reported as having been given in the same terms to those before him. A parallel statement at 6:88 says of a list of earlier prophets that had they associated, their deeds would have gone to waste. The Quran states the condition in both places without ever suggesting that any of them met it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are established at once. The standard does not soften for the person delivering it, which rules out any idea that carrying revelation is a privilege exempting its bearer. And the alternative to association is named as gratitude rather than as correct doctrine. That puts the surah's whole argument on a particular footing: recognising where a thing came from is treated as the root, and the rest follows from it.

crossReferences.why: Says of earlier prophets that association would have wasted their deeds, in the same conditional form.
States earlier in this surah that God does not approve ingratitude but approves thankfulness in His servants.
Attaches increase to thankfulness directly, in a proclamation made to an earlier community.

studies.applyIt: Say one specific thank you out loud today, to God, for something small enough that you have never mentioned it: a working knee, a quiet hour, a friend who answered. The root behind the word for thankfulness in this ayah is about fullness that shows on the outside, so say it aloud rather than only meaning it.

studies.title: They Did Not Measure Him
studies.meaning: The charge is a failure of estimation: they did not appraise God at His true appraisal. Two images of scale follow. The whole earth is a handful in His grasp on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens are rolled up like something put away. The sentence then declares Him beyond and above whatever they associate with Him, and the classical commentators treat that closing declaration as governing how the images are taken, since a being beyond all comparison cannot be pictured by the hand just mentioned.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has spent its length dismantling a devotion that treated lesser powers as effective, and here it names the underlying error as a mistake about size rather than about existence. The same charge, in identical wording, opens two other passages of the Quran, once against people who denied that God sends revelation to a human being. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah.

keyTerms.note: The root covers estimating a quantity, having power, and setting a decree. The charge is therefore not disbelief but mis-estimation, a wrong reading of size, made by people who did accept that God exists.
A noun for what a closed hand holds and for the act of closing it. It occurs once in the Quran, and its everyday use is of a small quantity taken up between the fingers.

A passive participle from the verb for rolling a scroll or folding a garment for storage. It occurs once in the Quran and belongs to the vocabulary of putting things away rather than of destroying them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Written documents were scrolls, and a scroll was rolled and tied when its matter was closed. Grain and dates were taken up by the handful and the scoop before anything was weighed. Both images in this ayah come from ordinary handling: something small enough to hold in one hand, and something finished enough to put away on a shelf. The scale is doing the work, not the strangeness.
studies.didYouKnow: The charge that opens this ayah, that they did not appraise God at His true appraisal, occurs three times in the Quran, here and at 6:91 and 22:74. Both of the others are followed at once by an argument about power: at 6:91 about whether God speaks to human beings at all, and at 22:74 about the weakness of what people call upon.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The root error is located in scale rather than in belief. The people addressed accepted that God made the world; what they had wrong was how much room that left for anything else to matter. Closing with a declaration that God is above what they associate does two jobs at once. It disposes of the partners, and it fixes the reading of the two images, which are given as measurements rather than as portraits.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the identical charge, there against the claim that God sent nothing down to any human being.
Uses the same sentence and follows it immediately with a statement of God's strength and might.
Gives the same image of the heaven folded, compared there to the rolling up of a written scroll.

studies.applyIt: Take the thing you currently treat as immovable: an institution, a market, a diagnosis, someone's settled decision. Hold it in mind and read this ayah's middle clause, where the entire earth is a handful. You are not being asked to think your problem is small. You are being asked to notice that you had been treating it as the largest item in view.

studies.title: The Trumpet Sounded Twice
studies.meaning: Two blasts and one exception. At the first, everyone in the heavens and the earth is struck down, except whom God wills, and the exception is left unexplained; the commentators offer several readings of who is spared and set them side by side without deciding. At the second, they are on their feet and looking. The Arabic marks no interval between the blasts beyond a single connective, so the whole scene arrives and reverses inside one sentence.
