studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Being raised after death was the part of the message most openly ridiculed in the city, and this surah has already quoted people laughing at it. Placing the trumpet here, straight after the ayah about God's true measure, connects the two: the objection to resurrection was in the end an objection about scale. No specific occasion is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A curved horn used for signalling across distance, the instrument that summoned a camp or announced an arrival. Commentators differ over its nature and agree on its function, which is to call people together.
From the word for a thunderbolt. The verb covers being stunned, falling senseless and dying, and the Quran uses it of Moses falling at the mountain, so the range is deliberate.
A plural noun rather than a verb, so it states a posture instead of an action. Nobody is described as rising; the second half of the ayah simply finds them already up and looking.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sound carried news in a landscape without walls. A horn or a shout from high ground called a camp to assemble, warned of a raid, or announced a returning caravan, and everyone knew which signal was which. One blast could empty a settlement into the open within minutes. The image needed no explaining to that audience; it needed only to be given the right scale.
studies.didYouKnow: The blowing of the trumpet is mentioned in around ten places across the Quran, but the two blasts are rarely set in a single sentence as they are here. The verb for what happens at the first is built from the word for a thunderbolt, and the same verb describes Moses falling senseless at the mountain at 7:143.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exception in the middle is the most interesting clause in the ayah. Everything is levelled except whom God wills, which inserts a reservation into a total statement and then leaves it unfilled. The tradition records more than one reading and does not settle it. What is asserted is not a list of survivors but that even the end has an exception in it, and that the exception belongs to God rather than to a rule.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same blast with the same reservation, everyone in terror except whom God wills.
Gives the second blast on its own, with people hurrying out of the graves toward their Lord.
The ayah before, whose statement about God's true measure this scene puts into action.

studies.applyIt: Pick a sound that reliably stops you: a phone ringing at an odd hour, an alarm, a knock you were not expecting. Notice what your body does in the half second before you know what it is. That half second is the only part of this ayah you have any access to now, and paying attention to it once is enough for today.

studies.title: The Earth Will Shine
studies.meaning: Five short clauses in sequence, each a stage of a court convening. The earth shines with the light of its Lord; the record is set down; the prophets and the witnesses are brought; judgement is given between them in truth; and they are not wronged. Commentators differ over who the witnesses are, some reading each community's own prophet and others those who testify to deeds, and they record the range. The light comes first, before any document or testimony, which is the order worth noticing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been arguing for a reckoning in front of people who denied there would be one, and this ayah answers by describing its procedure rather than its terror. The details are legal: illumination, a written record produced, witnesses called, a verdict given, and a guarantee against injustice. The audience knew all five stages from their own arbitrations. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: The verb used of the sun rising and flooding a place with light; the ordinary Arabic word for the east comes from the same root. It occurs once in the Quran and describes light arriving rather than being kindled.
A verb for placing something in front of people, used of laying out goods and of putting down a load. It makes the record an object in the room rather than a figure for knowledge.
The plural covers those who testify in a hearing and those who gave their lives, since both are people who stood publicly for something. Commentators read the word here in more than one way.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arbitration was held by daylight and in the open, in front of a gathering, and a case heard at night was suspect for that reason alone. Written records existed but were rare and expensive; most testimony was spoken and rested on the standing of the men who gave it. A hearing that opens with the ground itself lit, a written record produced and witnesses brought forward describes every guarantee their own system struggled to provide.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for the earth shining occurs once in the Quran, and it comes from the same root as the ordinary word for the east, the direction light arrives from. The ayah puts the illumination first and the written record second, so the whole place is lit before anything is read out, which reverses the order of any human court.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Judgement is presented as a procedure with safeguards rather than as an overwhelming event. There is a record, there are witnesses, there is a verdict in truth, and there is an explicit guarantee that nobody is wronged. That last clause is not decoration; it answers the fear that a reckoning conducted by absolute power would be arbitrary. The light that opens the scene sets the terms, since nothing in the proceeding happens in the dark.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same record set down, with people alarmed that it has left nothing out.
Asks how it will be when a witness is brought from every community, and one witness over them all.
The last ayah of this surah repeats this ayah's clause about judgement given in truth.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you were judged unfairly in a small way: a decision taken without the facts, a story told about you that stuck. Read the last four words of this ayah with that in mind. The guarantee against being wronged is placed at the very end of the sentence, after everything else, which is exactly where you would have put it.

studies.title: Paid In Full For What It Did
studies.meaning: A short ayah turning on an unusual verb: every soul is paid in full for what it did. The verb is the one used for settling a debt to the last unit, and it is passive, so nobody is named as the payer. Then a clause that looks redundant and is not: He knows best what they do. Commentators read it as covering what a record cannot show, since paying in full requires knowledge of the whole transaction, including what no witness could ever have reported.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following directly on the description of the court convening. The surah has been answering an audience who thought a reckoning either would not happen at all or could not possibly be fair. This ayah answers the second worry in a single line. The commentators read it together with the guarantee at the end of the previous ayah that nobody will be wronged, and treat the two as one statement.

keyTerms.gloss: and it was paid in full
keyTerms.note: An intensive passive from the root for fulfilling and completing, the ordinary verb for discharging a debt entirely. The intensive form rules out approximation and rules out a settlement at a discount.
An indefinite singular under a word meaning every, which in Arabic distributes a statement one by one rather than treating people as a mass. The payment is made individual by the grammar itself.
A general verb for doing, wider than the one used earlier in the same ayah for what was performed. The shift lets the second clause reach past what the first has just described.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wages were often settled at the end of a job and paid in kind, and disputes over the final measure were common: a labourer, a guide, a man hired for a season would argue about what had been agreed. The strongest thing that could be said of an employer was that he paid in full without having to be pressed. This ayah borrows that reputation and applies it at the largest possible scale.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb in this ayah is an intensive form of the root behind the word for keeping a promise, and behind the verb used earlier in this surah for God taking souls at death. The same root therefore covers being paid completely and being collected completely, a connection the Arabic makes in one word and English cannot.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passive form matters. No payer is named, so the sentence reads as a description of how things are settled rather than as a threat issued by someone. And the added clause about God knowing what they do quietly extends the reckoning past evidence. A court can pay out only on what is shown to it; this one pays on what is true, which is a claim about knowledge before it is a claim about fairness.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same clause inside a question about the Day, each soul paid in full and none wronged.
Closes the Quran's longest passage with the same promise of full payment and no wrong done.
The ayah before, which guarantees that judgement is given in truth and nobody is wronged.

studies.applyIt: Think of one piece of work you did well that nobody noticed, and one you got more credit for than it deserved. Hold both at once. The promise here is not that the first will be publicised but that the accounting will be complete, which includes the second. Let both halves land before you decide how the promise feels.

studies.title: Did No Messengers Come To You
studies.meaning: The scene is procedural rather than lurid. Those who refused are driven to Hell in throngs, the gates are opened, and the keepers put one question: did messengers not come to you from among yourselves, reciting your Lord's signs and warning you of this meeting? The answer is yes. Commentators note that the question is not asked to gather information but to establish the record in front of the people it concerns, and that the reply concedes everything without attempting a defence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside the long closing scene of the surah. Opponents in the city had repeatedly demanded an angel or an unmistakable sign instead of a man, and the question put by the keepers answers that in advance: the messengers were from among yourselves, which is exactly the objection those opponents had raised about the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). No occasion is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: The verb used for driving animals to water or to market, moving a group along rather than escorting it. It occurs twice in this surah, once for each of the two groups described.
A plural for bands of people arriving separately rather than as one crowd. It occurs twice in the Quran, both times in this surah, and the surah takes its name from the word.
From the root for storing and guarding a treasury. The keepers are custodians rather than tormentors, which is why the question they put is administrative in tone rather than cruel.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everyone knew the difference between being escorted and being driven. Livestock went to market in bands with each family's stock kept together, and a captive train after a raid moved the same way. The picture of people arriving at a gate in separate groups and being met by officials with a question was the shape of every arrival at a walled town, and the surah uses it twice, once for each destination.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for throngs occurs twice in the whole Quran, both in this surah, here and two ayat later of the other group; the surah takes its title from it. The word for the keepers at the gate occurs four times, twice in this surah and again at 40:49 and 67:8, always of officials stationed at an entrance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The question at the gate makes the entire procedure turn on notice. What is established is not the offence but the delivery: messengers came, from among your own people, reciting and warning. That puts responsibility where this surah has kept it throughout, with people who had the information. The answer matters too. Nobody argues, the record is conceded, and the passage stages no defeat because there is no contest.

crossReferences.why: The matching scene two ayat later, where the same driving and the same gates are met with a greeting.
Puts almost this exact question to humans and jinn, and has them testify against themselves.
Asks the same question at the same gate and records the same admission that a warner came.

studies.applyIt: Notice today one thing you already know you should do and have not scheduled. You are not short of information about it; nobody ever is. The question asked at the gate in this ayah is only about whether word arrived. Write the thing down with a day beside it, and let the record for that one item be different.

studies.title: The Lodging Of The Arrogant
studies.meaning: Two sentences, and the second is a comment rather than a continuation. Enter the gates of Hell, remaining there; then, how wretched is the lodging of the arrogant. That second sentence is not addressed to them. Commentators note that the verdict names a class rather than individuals, and names a disposition rather than a deed, which matches the surah's habit of closing a scene with a category. The word for lodging is the ordinary one for where a traveller stops on a journey.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the first of the surah's two final scenes. The people described are the same ones named earlier for inventing about God and for treating the message as a joke, and this ayah supplies their summary word. The commentators read the phrase about the arrogant as picking up an earlier ayah in this surah that asked whether Hell has no place for them. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A plural imperative, and the same verb used in the parallel scene addressed to the other group. Both destinations are entered by the same word, so nothing in the vocabulary of the command itself marks a difference.

From a root for lasting a very long time, used in Arabic of mountains and of a life that stretches on. The Quran uses it for both destinations, and it describes duration rather than a sentence handed down.
Where a traveller puts up, from a verb meaning to stay somewhere. Calling it a lodging is bleak precisely because a lodging implies a journey continuing afterwards, and this one does not.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A traveller's day ended at a lodging: a courtyard belonging to a relative, a corner of a market town where strangers were put up, a walled yard beside a well. The word carried an expectation, since nobody chose a lodging as a destination; it was where you stopped before going on. Applying it to a place with no onward road turned a familiar and mildly comforting word into something else entirely.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one that follows it use the same imperative for entering and the same word for remaining, for both destinations. The difference between the two scenes lies almost entirely in what the keepers at the gate say: a question in the first, and a greeting of peace in the second. The vocabulary is held constant so that the contrast falls on the speech.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ending a scene with a category rather than with names lets a reader test himself against a disposition instead of comparing himself with individuals. Arrogance is also a strange thing to name at a gate, since the people described are no longer in a position to assert anything at all. What the word identifies is the posture that produced everything else, and the passage offers it as the summary of a whole life.

crossReferences.why: Names the same class earlier in this surah, asking whether Hell has no place for the arrogant.
The matching ayah, where the same two words appear and the greeting given at the gate is peace.
Closes another passage with almost the identical formula about the residence of the arrogant.

studies.applyIt: Catch one moment this week when you turn down something useful because taking it would mean admitting you were wrong. That is the disposition this ayah names, in a size you can still do something about. You do not have to accept the thing. Just notice that the reason you refused had nothing to do with the thing itself.

studies.title: Its Gates Are Opened
studies.meaning: The scene mirrors the one two ayat earlier, and the small differences carry the sense. Both groups are led in throngs. Both reach gates. Both are met by keepers. But there the keepers ask a question, and here they give a greeting. In the middle of that greeting is a single word meaning you have come out good. Early scholars read it as a statement about a process ending, not as a compliment. What needed removing has been removed, and the door is what follows.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the closing part of the surah. The surah takes its name from the throngs described in these two matching scenes. It has argued throughout that people who agree about God's existence still split over what follows from it. The ending stages that split as two crowds moving in opposite directions. Few passages in the Quran hold a parallel this long.

keyTerms.note: Successive crowds rather than one mass, from a root suggesting a small sound gathering into more. The surah takes its name from this word, which is used of both processions equally.
From the word for a storehouse and what is kept in it. The same term is used of the keepers at the other gate, so the office is identical and only the words spoken differ.
From a root covering what is wholesome, clean and pleasant, used of good soil and of a sweet smell. It states a condition arrived at rather than praising a performance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A walled town had gates and gatekeepers who decided who came in. Arriving late meant waiting outside until morning. A stranger was asked about his business and his people before the gate moved. Everyone who travelled knew that pause at a wall. The greeting spoken here by the men at the gate is the ordinary greeting of peace. That is just what a traveller in that world most wanted to hear.
studies.didYouKnow: The two descriptions differ by one small joining word in the Arabic. It is present in this ayah and absent in its parallel. Early scholars have discussed it at length and read it in more than one way. Some take it to mean these gates stood open before the arrival, rather than being opened at it. Others treat it as ordinary style and draw nothing from it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Entry is described as arrival at a door, not as a payment collected. The last words spoken before it are a greeting. The keepers call them good on arrival, not at the start. So the journey itself is what produced the state they arrive in. The two scenes are given the same shape on purpose. A huge difference in outcome is then carried by very small differences in wording.

crossReferences.why: Gives the mirror scene, with the same procession, the same gates and a question instead of a greeting.
Shows the angels entering with the same greeting, naming what it is given for: peace, for your patience.
Sets both groups within sight of each other and lets them speak, which this pair of scenes does not.

studies.applyIt: The greeting at the gate in this ayah is the ordinary one, the same words you would use at a door. Say it properly to the next three people you meet: not muttered, not shortened, with your attention on them for the second it takes. It is the sentence this passage puts at the threshold of everything.
studies.explainEasier: People who were careful about their Lord are led to Paradise in groups. The gates are opened for them. The gatekeepers say, Peace be on you. You have turned out good, so come in and stay for good.

studies.title: He Kept His Promise To Us
studies.meaning: The first words spoken inside are praise, and what is praised is precise: God was true to us in His promise. Then a claim of inheritance, that they were made to inherit the land, and then a freedom, that they settle wherever in the Garden they wish. Commentators discuss which land is meant, some reading the ground of the Garden itself and others the earth promised to righteous servants, and they preserve both. The ayah ends with a comment on the wage of those who worked.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the very end of the surah's closing scene, spoken by people who have just come through the gate. The community hearing this in Mecca had been promised a great deal and could point to none of it yet. Several passages of these years answer that gap by projecting forward to the moment when the promise is acknowledged as kept. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: The verb takes both a person and a thing, so it means He proved truthful to us in the matter of His promise. It is the same root as truthfulness, applied to a promise honoured rather than a statement made.
The verb for passing property to heirs. Inheritance implies a previous holder and a transfer at a set time, which is why the commentators discuss carefully what is being handed over here.

keyTerms.gloss: we settle, we take our place
keyTerms.note: A verb for choosing a place to live and making it your own, used of a household setting up. It occurs once in the Quran in this form, and it grants a choice rather than an assignment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Land in Arabia was rarely owned outright by ordinary people. Grazing was seasonal and negotiated, wells belonged to clans, and a family's right to a place rested on agreements that could lapse with a quarrel. Inheriting land and then choosing freely where inside it to settle described two things most of that audience had never had in their lives: secure title, and freedom of movement within it.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for settling wherever they wish occurs once in the Quran in this form, and the phrase about being made to inherit the land appears only here. Both are unusual choices for a description of the Garden, and both are drawn from the vocabulary of property and tenure rather than from the vocabulary of pleasure.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What is praised first is not the place but the keeping of a promise, which puts the weight on God's reliability rather than on the reward. That matches the assurance given much earlier in the same surah that God does not fail an appointment. The freedom at the end is worth noticing too: the reward includes choosing, which is precisely the faculty that was under pressure throughout the argument the surah has been having.

crossReferences.why: Makes the promise this ayah acknowledges as kept, closing with the line that God never fails an appointment.
States that righteous servants will inherit the earth, quoted there from an earlier scripture.
Records the same first words from people entering, praise to God who guided them to this.

studies.applyIt: Think of a promise someone kept to you when it would have been easy not to, and how that landed at the time. Then thank God for one thing He has already delivered on, in those exact terms: not for the gift but for the keeping of the word. It is a different sentence from the usual one, and it lands differently too.

studies.title: Angels Encircling The Throne
studies.meaning: The surah ends by pulling back. Angels are seen ringing the Throne on every side, glorifying their Lord with praise, and then one clause repeats what was said six ayat earlier, that judgement is given between them in truth. The final words are the same phrase that opens the Quran's first surah. Commentators note the framing: the scene has moved from crowds at gates to a quiet ring, and what closes it is an act of praise rather than a verdict.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, the last ayah of a surah that has spent its whole length arguing with one city. The commentators observe that its closing praise matches the praise that opens the Book, and read the ending as a deliberate return rather than a conclusion. The audience had been promised a reckoning and told repeatedly it would come; the surah ends by showing it finished and the noise gone. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A participle from a verb meaning to surround something on every side, related to the word for a border or a hem. It occurs once in the Quran, and it describes a ring rather than a crowd.
From a root for swimming or moving freely through water. Glorification is pictured as continuous motion around something rather than as a set of words being repeated on cue.
A plural taking in every category of created thing, not only humanity. The surah closes with the widest word available to it, after arguing at length with the people of a single town.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A ruler in that world was known by his circle. Petitioners saw the ring of men around a seated chief before they saw the chief himself, and the size and bearing of that ring told them what they were dealing with. Councils met seated in a circle, and the word for such an assembly came from sitting round. The final image here uses a shape its audience read instinctively as settled authority.
studies.didYouKnow: The last words of this surah are the same words that open the first surah of the Quran. The verb describing the angels ringing the Throne occurs once in the whole Book. And the surah's final clause about judgement given in truth repeats, word for word, the clause used six ayat earlier, so the ending is assembled almost entirely out of repetitions.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ending on praise rather than on the verdict changes what a reader is left holding. The judgement is stated in a subordinate clause and passed over, while what fills the last line is worship continuing around a throne, unaffected by the argument that has just concluded. That places the whole dispute of the surah in proportion. It mattered enormously, it is over, and what continues was never interrupted by it.

crossReferences.why: The Quran's opening surah uses the same words with which this surah closes.
Describes those who carry the Throne and those around it glorifying and asking forgiveness for believers.
The earlier ayah whose clause about judgement given in truth is repeated word for word here.

studies.applyIt: End something today with praise instead of a verdict: a hard conversation, a task that went badly, a day you would rather not review. Say one honest good thing about it aloud and then stop, without adding the assessment you were about to add. This surah closes that way after seventy-five ayat of argument, and it is a usable habit.
